Hence! home, you idle creatures, get you home. / Is this a holiday? What, know you not, / Being mechanical, you ought not walk / Upon a labouring day without the sign / Of your profession? Speak, what trade art thou?

Go away! Home, you lazy lot, go home. Is this a holiday? What, don't you know that, as working men, you're not supposed to walk about on a working day without the tools of your trade? You, what's your trade?
Where is thy leather apron and thy rule? / What dost thou with thy best apparel on? / You, sir, what trade are you?
Where's your leather apron and your ruler? Why are you wearing your best clothes? You, sir, what's your trade?
Truly, sir, in respect of a fine workman, I am but, as you would say, a / cobbler.
Well, sir, compared with a fine craftsman, I'm only, as you might say, a cobbler.
But what trade art thou? Answer me directly.
But what's your trade? Give me a straight answer.
A trade, sir, that I hope I may use with a safe conscience, which is / indeed, sir, a mender of bad soles.
A trade, sir, that I hope I can practise with a clear conscience. I'm a mender of bad soles, sir.
What trade, thou knave? Thou naughty knave, what trade?
What trade, you rascal? You good-for-nothing, what trade?
Nay, I beseech you, sir, be not out with me; yet, if you be out, sir, I / can mend you.
Now, please, sir, don't be cross with me. Still, if your soles are worn out, sir, I can mend you.
What mean'st thou by that? Mend me, thou saucy fellow!
What do you mean by that? Mend me, you cheeky fellow!
Thou art a cobbler, art thou?

Truly, sir, all that I live by is with the awl; I meddle with no / tradesman's matters, nor women's matters, but withal I am indeed, sir, / a surgeon to old shoes: when they are in great danger, I recover them. / As proper men as ever trod upon neat's leather have gone upon my / handiwork.

Honestly, sir, all I live by is the awl. I don't meddle in other tradesmen's business or in women's business, but I am, sir, a surgeon to old shoes: when they're in great danger, I bring them back to health. As fine men as ever walked on cowhide have walked on my work.
But wherefore art not in thy shop today? / Why dost thou lead these men about the streets?
But why aren't you in your shop today? Why are you leading these men about the streets?
Truly, sir, to wear out their shoes, to get myself into more work. But / indeed, sir, we make holiday to see Caesar, and to rejoice in his / triumph.
Honestly, sir, to wear out their shoes and get myself more work. But really, sir, we're taking a holiday to see Caesar and celebrate his triumph.

Wherefore rejoice? What conquest brings he home? / What tributaries follow him to Rome, / To grace in captive bonds his chariot wheels? / You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things! / O you hard hearts, you cruel men of Rome, / Knew you not Pompey? Many a time and oft / Have you climb'd up to walls and battlements, / To towers and windows, yea, to chimney tops, / Your infants in your arms, and there have sat / The livelong day with patient expectation, / To see great Pompey pass the streets of Rome. / And when you saw his chariot but appear, / Have you not made an universal shout, / That Tiber trembled underneath her banks / To hear the replication of your sounds / Made in her concave shores? / And do you now put on your best attire? / And do you now cull out a holiday? / And do you now strew flowers in his way, / That comes in triumph over Pompey's blood? / Be gone! / Run to your houses, fall upon your knees, / Pray to the gods to intermit the plague / That needs must light on this ingratitude.

Celebrate what? What conquest is he bringing home? What captive kings follow him to Rome, chained to his chariot wheels to decorate his parade? You blocks, you stones, you are worse than senseless things! You hard-hearted, cruel men of Rome, didn't you know Pompey? Many times you climbed up onto walls and battlements, towers and windows, even chimney tops, with your babies in your arms, and sat there all day waiting patiently to see great Pompey pass through the streets of Rome. And when you saw just his chariot appear, didn't you shout together so loudly that the Tiber trembled in its banks to hear the echo of your noise in its hollow shores? And now you put on your best clothes? And now you pick out a holiday? And now you scatter flowers in the path of the man who comes in triumph over Pompey's blood? Go! Run home, fall on your knees, and pray to the gods to hold back the punishment that is sure to fall on such ingratitude.

Go, go, good countrymen, and, for this fault / Assemble all the poor men of your sort, / Draw them to Tiber banks, and weep your tears / Into the channel, till the lowest stream / Do kiss the most exalted shores of all.

Go, go, good countrymen, and to make up for this fault, gather all the poor men like you, take them to the banks of the Tiber, and weep your tears into the river until even its lowest water rises to touch the top of its banks.

See whether their basest metal be not mov'd; / They vanish tongue-tied in their guiltiness. / Go you down that way towards the Capitol; / This way will I. Disrobe the images, / If you do find them deck'd with ceremonies.

See if even their dull metal isn't moved. They slink away, tongue-tied with guilt. You go down that way towards the Capitol; I'll go this way. Strip the statues if you find them decorated for the celebrations.
May we do so? / You know it is the feast of Lupercal.
Are we allowed to? You know it's the feast of Lupercal.

It is no matter; let no images / Be hung with Caesar's trophies. I'll about / And drive away the vulgar from the streets; / So do you too, where you perceive them thick. / These growing feathers pluck'd from Caesar's wing / Will make him fly an ordinary pitch, / Who else would soar above the view of men, / And keep us all in servile fearfulness.

It doesn't matter. Don't let any statues be hung with Caesar's trophies. I'll go round and clear the common people off the streets, and you do the same wherever you see them crowding. If we pluck these growing feathers from Caesar's wing, he'll fly at an ordinary height. Otherwise he would soar out of sight of men and keep us all in fear like slaves.
Stand you directly in Antonius' way, / When he doth run his course. Antonius.
Stand right in Antonius's path when he runs his race. Antonius.
Forget not in your speed, Antonius, / To touch Calphurnia; for our elders say, / The barren, touched in this holy chase, / Shake off their sterile curse.
Don't forget, Antonius, as you run, to touch Calphurnia. Our elders say that childless women who are touched in this holy race lose their curse of barrenness.
I shall remember. / When Caesar says "Do this," it is perform'd.
I'll remember. When Caesar says "Do this," it is done.
Set on; and leave no ceremony out.
Go on, and leave out none of the ceremonies.
Bid every noise be still; peace yet again!
Make every noise stop. Quiet again!
Who is it in the press that calls on me? / I hear a tongue shriller than all the music, / Cry "Caesar"! Speak. Caesar is turn'd to hear.
Who in the crowd is calling me? I hear a voice shriller than all the music cry "Caesar!" Speak. Caesar has turned to listen.
A soothsayer bids you beware the Ides of March.
A fortune-teller tells you to beware the fifteenth of March.
Set him before me; let me see his face.
Bring him in front of me. Let me see his face.
Fellow, come from the throng; look upon Caesar.
You, come out of the crowd. Look at Caesar.
What say'st thou to me now? Speak once again.
What do you say to me now? Say it again.
He is a dreamer; let us leave him. Pass.
He's a dreamer. Let's leave him. Move on.
Will you go see the order of the course?
Are you going to watch the race?
I am not gamesome: I do lack some part / Of that quick spirit that is in Antony. / Let me not hinder, Cassius, your desires; / I'll leave you.
I'm not in the mood for games. I lack some of the lively spirit that Antony has. Don't let me stop you doing what you want, Cassius. I'll leave you.

Brutus, I do observe you now of late: / I have not from your eyes that gentleness / And show of love as I was wont to have. / You bear too stubborn and too strange a hand / Over your friend that loves you.
Brutus, I've been watching you lately. I don't see the gentleness and signs of affection in your eyes that I used to. You're too cold and distant with a friend who loves you.

Cassius, / Be not deceived: if I have veil'd my look, / I turn the trouble of my countenance / Merely upon myself. Vexed I am / Of late with passions of some difference, / Conceptions only proper to myself, / Which give some soil perhaps to my behaviors; / But let not therefore my good friends be grieved / (Among which number, Cassius, be you one) / Nor construe any further my neglect, / Than that poor Brutus, with himself at war, / Forgets the shows of love to other men.

Cassius, don't be misled. If I've looked troubled, my frown is aimed only at myself. Lately I have been troubled by conflicting feelings, thoughts that concern only me, which perhaps spoil my behaviour a little. But don't let my good friends be upset by it (and you are one of them, Cassius), or read anything more into my neglect than that poor Brutus, at war with himself, forgets to show his affection to other men.
Then, Brutus, I have much mistook your passion; / By means whereof this breast of mine hath buried / Thoughts of great value, worthy cogitations. / Tell me, good Brutus, can you see your face?
Then, Brutus, I have badly misread your feelings, and because of that I have kept to myself some thoughts of great importance, very serious ideas. Tell me, good Brutus, can you see your own face?
No, Cassius, for the eye sees not itself / But by reflection, by some other thing.
No, Cassius, because the eye can't see itself except by reflection, in something else.

'Tis just: / And it is very much lamented, Brutus, / That you have no such mirrors as will turn / Your hidden worthiness into your eye, / That you might see your shadow. I have heard / Where many of the best respect in Rome, / (Except immortal Caesar) speaking of Brutus, / And groaning underneath this age's yoke, / Have wish'd that noble Brutus had his eyes.

That's right. And it's a great pity, Brutus, that you have no mirrors that could show your hidden worth to your own eyes, so you could see your reflection. I have heard many of the most respected men in Rome (except immortal Caesar), speaking of Brutus and groaning under the oppression of these times, wish that noble Brutus could see himself as they do.
Into what dangers would you lead me, Cassius, / That you would have me seek into myself / For that which is not in me?
What danger are you leading me into, Cassius, that you want me to look inside myself for something that isn't there?

Therefore, good Brutus, be prepared to hear; / And since you know you cannot see yourself / So well as by reflection, I, your glass, / Will modestly discover to yourself / That of yourself which you yet know not of. / And be not jealous on me, gentle Brutus: / Were I a common laugher, or did use / To stale with ordinary oaths my love / To every new protester; if you know / That I do fawn on men, and hug them hard, / And after scandal them; or if you know / That I profess myself in banqueting, / To all the rout, then hold me dangerous.

So, good Brutus, get ready to listen. And since you know you can't see yourself as well as by reflection, I will be your mirror and modestly show you the part of yourself you don't yet know about. And don't be suspicious of me, gentle Brutus. If I were a common joker, or cheapened my friendship by swearing it to every new person who claimed to be my friend; if you know that I flatter men and hug them hard and then slander them behind their backs; or if you know that I declare friendship to all the riff-raff when I'm feasting, then consider me dangerous.
What means this shouting? I do fear the people / Choose Caesar for their king.
What's this shouting for? I'm afraid the people are choosing Caesar as their king.
Ay, do you fear it? / Then must I think you would not have it so.
Oh, are you afraid of it? Then I must think you wouldn't want it to happen.

I would not, Cassius; yet I love him well, / But wherefore do you hold me here so long? / What is it that you would impart to me? / If it be aught toward the general good, / Set honour in one eye and death i' the other, / And I will look on both indifferently; / For let the gods so speed me as I love / The name of honour more than I fear death.

I wouldn't, Cassius. And yet I love him well. But why are you keeping me here so long? What is it you want to tell me? If it is anything for the public good, set honour in front of one eye and death in front of the other, and I will look at both without caring which. Let the gods only bless me as much as I love the name of honour more than I fear death.

I know that virtue to be in you, Brutus, / As well as I do know your outward favour. / Well, honour is the subject of my story. / I cannot tell what you and other men / Think of this life; but, for my single self, / I had as lief not be as live to be / In awe of such a thing as I myself. / I was born free as Caesar; so were you; / We both have fed as well, and we can both / Endure the winter's cold as well as he: / For once, upon a raw and gusty day, / The troubled Tiber chafing with her shores, / Caesar said to me, "Dar'st thou, Cassius, now / Leap in with me into this angry flood, / And swim to yonder point?" Upon the word, / Accoutred as I was, I plunged in, / And bade him follow: so indeed he did. / The torrent roar'd, and we did buffet it / With lusty sinews, throwing it aside / And stemming it with hearts of controversy. / But ere we could arrive the point propos'd, / Caesar cried, "Help me, Cassius, or I sink!" / I, as Aeneas, our great ancestor, / Did from the flames of Troy upon his shoulder / The old Anchises bear, so from the waves of Tiber / Did I the tired Caesar. And this man / Is now become a god; and Cassius is / A wretched creature, and must bend his body, / If Caesar carelessly but nod on him. / He had a fever when he was in Spain, / And when the fit was on him I did mark / How he did shake: 'tis true, this god did shake: / His coward lips did from their colour fly, / And that same eye whose bend doth awe the world / Did lose his lustre. I did hear him groan: / Ay, and that tongue of his, that bade the Romans / Mark him, and write his speeches in their books, / Alas, it cried, "Give me some drink, Titinius," / As a sick girl. Ye gods, it doth amaze me, / A man of such a feeble temper should / So get the start of the majestic world, / And bear the palm alone.

I know you have that virtue, Brutus, as well as I know your face. Well, honour is the subject of my story. I can't say what you and other men think of this life, but for my part I would rather not exist than live in awe of a man no better than I am. I was born as free as Caesar, and so were you. We have both eaten as well as he has, and we can both stand the winter cold as well as he can. Once, on a raw, windy day, when the stormy Tiber was crashing against its banks, Caesar said to me, "Do you dare, Cassius, to leap into this angry river with me now and swim to that point over there?" At that, dressed as I was, I plunged in and told him to follow, and so he did. The torrent roared, and we fought it with strong muscles, throwing it aside and pushing against it with competitive hearts. But before we could reach the point, Caesar cried, "Help me, Cassius, or I'll sink!" Just as Aeneas, our great ancestor, carried old Anchises out of the flames of Troy on his shoulder, so I carried the tired Caesar out of the waves of the Tiber. And this man has now become a god, and Cassius is a wretched creature who must bow down if Caesar even carelessly nods at him. He had a fever when he was in Spain, and when the fit was on him I saw how he shook. It's true: this god shook. His cowardly lips lost their colour, and that same eye whose glance terrifies the world lost its shine. I heard him groan. Yes, and that tongue of his, which ordered the Romans to listen to him and write his speeches down in their books, cried, "Give me a drink, Titinius," like a sick girl. You gods, it amazes me that a man with such a weak constitution should get ahead of the whole majestic world and carry off the victor's prize alone.
Another general shout? / I do believe that these applauses are / For some new honours that are heap'd on Caesar.
Another shout from everyone? I believe this applause is for some new honours being heaped on Caesar.

Why, man, he doth bestride the narrow world / Like a Colossus, and we petty men / Walk under his huge legs, and peep about / To find ourselves dishonourable graves. / Men at some time are masters of their fates: / The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings. / "Brutus" and "Caesar": what should be in that "Caesar"? / Why should that name be sounded more than yours? / Write them together, yours is as fair a name; / Sound them, it doth become the mouth as well; / Weigh them, it is as heavy; conjure with 'em, / "Brutus" will start a spirit as soon as "Caesar." / Now in the names of all the gods at once, / Upon what meat doth this our Caesar feed, / That he is grown so great? Age, thou art sham'd! / Rome, thou hast lost the breed of noble bloods! / When went there by an age since the great flood, / But it was fam'd with more than with one man? / When could they say, till now, that talk'd of Rome, / That her wide walls encompass'd but one man? / Now is it Rome indeed, and room enough, / When there is in it but one only man. / O, you and I have heard our fathers say, / There was a Brutus once that would have brook'd / Th' eternal devil to keep his state in Rome, / As easily as a king!

Why, man, he stands over the narrow world like a giant statue, and we little men walk under his huge legs and peer about to find ourselves shameful graves. At some point men are masters of their own fates. The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars but in ourselves, that we are underlings. "Brutus" and "Caesar": what is so special about "Caesar"? Why should that name be spoken more than yours? Write them side by side: yours is just as fine a name. Say them: yours sounds as good. Weigh them: it's as heavy. Use them in spells: "Brutus" will call up a spirit as fast as "Caesar." Now, in the names of all the gods at once, what food does this Caesar of ours eat that makes him grow so great? Our age should be ashamed! Rome, you have lost the breed of noble men! Since the great flood, was there ever an age that wasn't famous for more than one man? Until now, when could anyone talking of Rome say that her wide walls held only one man? Now it really is Rome, and room enough, when there's only one man in it. Oh, you and I have heard our fathers say that there was once a Brutus who would have let the devil himself rule in Rome as easily as he would have allowed a king.

That you do love me, I am nothing jealous; / What you would work me to, I have some aim: / How I have thought of this, and of these times, / I shall recount hereafter. For this present, / I would not, so with love I might entreat you, / Be any further mov'd. What you have said, / I will consider; what you have to say / I will with patience hear; and find a time / Both meet to hear and answer such high things. / Till then, my noble friend, chew upon this: / Brutus had rather be a villager / Than to repute himself a son of Rome / Under these hard conditions as this time / Is like to lay upon us.

I don't doubt at all that you love me. I have some idea what you want to persuade me to do. What I think about this, and about these times, I'll tell you later. For now, I ask you as a friend, don't push me any further. I will think about what you have said; I will listen patiently to whatever else you have to say, and find a suitable time both to hear and answer such serious matters. Until then, my noble friend, think about this: Brutus would rather be a villager than call himself a son of Rome under the hard conditions these times are likely to put on us.
I am glad that my weak words / Have struck but thus much show of fire from Brutus.
I'm glad my weak words have struck even this much fire from Brutus.
The games are done, and Caesar is returning.
The games are over, and Caesar is coming back.
As they pass by, pluck Casca by the sleeve, / And he will, after his sour fashion, tell you / What hath proceeded worthy note today.
As they pass by, tug Casca's sleeve, and in his sour way he'll tell you what happened today that's worth knowing.

I will do so. But, look you, Cassius, / The angry spot doth glow on Caesar's brow, / And all the rest look like a chidden train: / Calphurnia's cheek is pale; and Cicero / Looks with such ferret and such fiery eyes / As we have seen him in the Capitol, / Being cross'd in conference by some senators.

I will. But look, Cassius, an angry red spot glows on Caesar's forehead, and all the rest look like servants who have been told off. Calphurnia's cheek is pale, and Cicero has the red, fiery eyes of a ferret, as we've seen him in the Capitol when senators disagree with him in debate.
Casca will tell us what the matter is.
Casca will tell us what's wrong.
Let me have men about me that are fat, / Sleek-headed men, and such as sleep a-nights: / Yond Cassius has a lean and hungry look; / He thinks too much: such men are dangerous.
I want men around me who are fat, men with smooth, well-groomed heads who sleep at night. That Cassius over there has a lean and hungry look. He thinks too much. Men like that are dangerous.
Fear him not, Caesar; he's not dangerous; / He is a noble Roman and well given.
Don't be afraid of him, Caesar, he's not dangerous. He's a noble Roman and well disposed to you.

Would he were fatter! But I fear him not: / Yet if my name were liable to fear, / I do not know the man I should avoid / So soon as that spare Cassius. He reads much, / He is a great observer, and he looks / Quite through the deeds of men. He loves no plays, / As thou dost, Antony; he hears no music. / Seldom he smiles; and smiles in such a sort / As if he mock'd himself and scorn'd his spirit / That could be mov'd to smile at anything. / Such men as he be never at heart's ease / Whiles they behold a greater than themselves, / And therefore are they very dangerous. / I rather tell thee what is to be fear'd / Than what I fear; for always I am Caesar. / Come on my right hand, for this ear is deaf, / And tell me truly what thou think'st of him.

I wish he were fatter! But I'm not afraid of him. Yet if Caesar could feel fear, I don't know any man I would avoid sooner than that thin Cassius. He reads a lot, he watches everything, and he sees right through what men do to their motives. He doesn't like plays, as you do, Antony; he doesn't listen to music. He rarely smiles, and when he does, it's as if he were mocking himself and despising his own spirit for being moved to smile at anything. Men like him are never comfortable while they see someone greater than themselves, and that's why they are very dangerous. I'm telling you what ought to be feared, not what I fear, because I am always Caesar. Come round to my right side, because this ear is deaf, and tell me honestly what you think of him.
You pull'd me by the cloak; would you speak with me?
You pulled my cloak. Do you want to talk to me?
Ay, Casca, tell us what hath chanc'd today, / That Caesar looks so sad.
Yes, Casca. Tell us what happened today to make Caesar look so serious.
Why, you were with him, were you not?
Why, you were with him, weren't you?
I should not then ask Casca what had chanc'd.
Then I wouldn't be asking Casca what happened.
Why, there was a crown offer'd him; and being offer'd him, he put it by / with the back of his hand, thus; and then the people fell a-shouting.
Well, he was offered a crown, and when it was offered he pushed it away with the back of his hand, like this, and then the people started shouting.
What was the second noise for?
What was the second shout for?
They shouted thrice: what was the last cry for?
They shouted three times. What was the last cheer for?
Was the crown offer'd him thrice?
Was he offered the crown three times?
Ay, marry, was't, and he put it by thrice, every time gentler than / other; and at every putting-by mine honest neighbours shouted.
Yes, by God, he was, and he pushed it away three times, each time more gently than the last, and every time he pushed it away my honest neighbours shouted.
Tell us the manner of it, gentle Casca.
Tell us how it happened, gentle Casca.

I can as well be hang'd, as tell the manner of it: it was mere foolery; / I did not mark it. I saw Mark Antony offer him a crown; yet 'twas not a / crown neither, 'twas one of these coronets; and, as I told you, he put / it by once: but, for all that, to my thinking, he would fain have had / it. Then he offered it to him again: then he put it by again: but, to / my thinking, he was very loath to lay his fingers off it. And then he / offered it the third time; he put it the third time by; and still, as / he refus'd it, the rabblement hooted, and clapp'd their chopt hands, / and threw up their sweaty night-caps, and uttered such a deal of / stinking breath because Caesar refus'd the crown, that it had, almost, / choked Caesar, for he swooned, and fell down at it. And for mine own / part, I durst not laugh, for fear of opening my lips and receiving the / bad air.

I might as well be hanged as tell you how it happened. It was pure nonsense; I didn't pay attention. I saw Mark Antony offer him a crown, though it wasn't really a crown, it was one of those little coronets, and, as I told you, he pushed it away once. But all the same, I think he'd have liked to have it. Then Antony offered it to him again, and he pushed it away again, but I think he was very unwilling to take his fingers off it. And then Antony offered it the third time, and he pushed it away the third time. And each time he refused it, the mob hooted and clapped their chapped hands and threw up their sweaty nightcaps, and let out such a quantity of stinking breath because Caesar refused the crown that it almost choked Caesar, because he fainted and fell down from it. And for my part, I didn't dare laugh, for fear of opening my lips and breathing in the bad air.
But, soft! I pray you. What, did Caesar swoon?
Wait, please. What, did Caesar faint?
He fell down in the market-place, and foam'd at mouth, and was / speechless.
He fell down in the market-place, foamed at the mouth and couldn't speak.
'Tis very like: he hath the falling-sickness.
That's very likely. He has epilepsy, the falling sickness.
No, Caesar hath it not; but you, and I, / And honest Casca, we have the falling-sickness.
No, Caesar doesn't have it. But you and I and honest Casca, we have the falling sickness.

I know not what you mean by that; but I am sure Caesar fell down. If / the tag-rag people did not clap him and hiss him, according as he / pleased and displeased them, as they use to do the players in the / theatre, I am no true man.

I don't know what you mean by that, but I'm sure Caesar fell down. If the ragged crowd didn't clap and hiss him according to whether he pleased or displeased them, just as they do to actors in the theatre, I'm no honest man.
What said he when he came unto himself?
What did he say when he came round?

Marry, before he fell down, when he perceived the common herd was glad / he refused the crown, he pluck'd me ope his doublet, and offer'd them / his throat to cut. And I had been a man of any occupation, if I would / not have taken him at a word, I would I might go to hell among the / rogues. And so he fell. When he came to himself again, he said, if he / had done or said anything amiss, he desir'd their worships to think it / was his infirmity. Three or four wenches where I stood cried, "Alas, / good soul!" and forgave him with all their hearts. But there's no heed / to be taken of them: if Caesar had stabb'd their mothers, they would / have done no less.

Well, before he fell down, when he saw the common herd was glad he refused the crown, he pulled open his jacket and offered them his throat to cut. If I had been a working man with a tool in my hand, I'd have taken him at his word, or I hope I go to hell with the scoundrels. And so he fell. When he came round again, he said that if he had done or said anything wrong, he wanted their worships to put it down to his illness. Three or four women near me cried, "Oh, the poor man!" and forgave him with all their hearts. But you can't take any notice of them: if Caesar had stabbed their mothers, they would have done the same.
And, after that, he came thus sad away?
And after that he came away this serious?

Nay, and I tell you that, I'll ne'er look you i' the face again. But / those that understood him smil'd at one another and shook their heads; / but for mine own part, it was Greek to me. I could tell you more news / too: Marullus and Flavius, for pulling scarfs off Caesar's images, are / put to silence. Fare you well. There was more foolery yet, if I could / remember it.

No, if I told you that, I'd never be able to look you in the face again. But those who understood him smiled at one another and shook their heads. As for me, it was Greek to me. I could tell you more news, too: Marullus and Flavius have been silenced for pulling the scarves off Caesar's statues. Goodbye. There was more foolery still, if I could remember it.
Will you sup with me tonight, Casca?
Will you have supper with me tonight, Casca?
No, I've already promised to go out.
Will you dine with me tomorrow?
Will you have dinner with me tomorrow?
Ay, if I be alive, and your mind hold, and your dinner worth the / eating.
Yes, if I'm alive, and you don't change your mind, and your dinner is worth eating.
What a blunt fellow is this grown to be! / He was quick mettle when he went to school.
What a blunt fellow he has turned into! He was so sharp when he was at school.

So is he now in execution / Of any bold or noble enterprise, / However he puts on this tardy form. / This rudeness is a sauce to his good wit, / Which gives men stomach to digest his words / With better appetite.

He still is when it comes to carrying out any bold or noble plan, though he puts on this slow manner. His rudeness is a sauce for his good sense: it gives people the appetite to swallow what he says with more pleasure.
And so it is. For this time I will leave you: / Tomorrow, if you please to speak with me, / I will come home to you; or, if you will, / Come home to me, and I will wait for you.
That's true. I'll leave you for now. Tomorrow, if you want to talk to me, I'll come to your house; or, if you like, come to mine and I'll wait for you.
I will do so: till then, think of the world.
I will. Until then, think about the state of the world.

Well, Brutus, thou art noble; yet I see, / Thy honourable metal may be wrought / From that it is dispos'd: therefore 'tis meet / That noble minds keep ever with their likes; / For who so firm that cannot be seduc'd? / Caesar doth bear me hard, but he loves Brutus. / If I were Brutus now, and he were Cassius, / He should not humour me. I will this night, / In several hands, in at his windows throw, / As if they came from several citizens, / Writings, all tending to the great opinion / That Rome holds of his name; wherein obscurely / Caesar's ambition shall be glanced at. / And after this, let Caesar seat him sure, / For we will shake him, or worse days endure.

Well, Brutus, you are noble. And yet I see your honourable metal can be bent away from its natural shape. So it's right that noble minds should always keep company with their own kind, because who is so firm that he can't be led astray? Caesar holds a grudge against me, but he loves Brutus. If I were Brutus now and he were Cassius, he wouldn't win me round. Tonight I will throw letters in through his windows in different handwriting, as if they came from different citizens, all about the high opinion Rome has of him, and hinting at Caesar's ambition. And after this, let Caesar sit tight, because we will shake him off, or suffer worse times.
Good even, Casca: brought you Caesar home? / Why are you breathless, and why stare you so?
Good evening, Casca. Did you bring Caesar home? Why are you out of breath, and why are you staring like that?

Are not you moved, when all the sway of earth / Shakes like a thing unfirm? O Cicero, / I have seen tempests, when the scolding winds / Have riv'd the knotty oaks; and I have seen / Th' ambitious ocean swell and rage and foam, / To be exalted with the threatening clouds: / But never till tonight, never till now, / Did I go through a tempest dropping fire. / Either there is a civil strife in heaven, / Or else the world too saucy with the gods, / Incenses them to send destruction.

Aren't you disturbed when the whole earth shakes as if it were unsteady? Oh, Cicero, I have seen storms when the howling winds have split the gnarled oaks, and I have seen the ambitious ocean swell and rage and foam to reach as high as the threatening clouds. But never until tonight, never until now, have I walked through a storm raining fire. Either there is civil war in heaven, or else the world has been so insolent to the gods that it has provoked them to destroy it.
Why, saw you anything more wonderful?
Why, did you see anything more amazing?

A common slave, you'd know him well by sight, / Held up his left hand, which did flame and burn / Like twenty torches join'd, and yet his hand, / Not sensible of fire remain'd unscorch'd. / Besides, I ha' not since put up my sword, / Against the Capitol I met a lion, / Who glared upon me, and went surly by, / Without annoying me. And there were drawn / Upon a heap a hundred ghastly women, / Transformed with their fear; who swore they saw / Men, all in fire, walk up and down the streets. / And yesterday the bird of night did sit, / Even at noonday upon the marketplace, / Hooting and shrieking. When these prodigies / Do so conjointly meet, let not men say, / "These are their reasons; they are natural"; / For I believe, they are portentous things / Unto the climate that they point upon.

A common slave, you'd know him by sight, held up his left hand, which flamed and burned like twenty torches put together, and yet his hand felt no fire and stayed unburnt. Besides that (I haven't put my sword away since), by the Capitol I met a lion, which glared at me and walked sullenly past without attacking me. And a hundred terrified women were huddled in a heap, changed out of all recognition by fear, who swore they saw men all on fire walking up and down the streets. And yesterday the owl, the bird of night, sat in the market-place even at midday, hooting and shrieking. When these unnatural signs all happen together, don't let anyone say, "There are reasons for them, they're natural," because I believe they are omens of disaster for the country they point to.
Indeed, it is a strange-disposed time. / But men may construe things after their fashion, / Clean from the purpose of the things themselves. / Comes Caesar to the Capitol tomorrow?
It certainly is a strange time. But men can interpret things in their own way, quite differently from what the things really mean. Is Caesar coming to the Capitol tomorrow?
He doth, for he did bid Antonius / Send word to you he would be there tomorrow.
He is. He told Antonius to send you word that he would be there tomorrow.
Goodnight then, Casca: this disturbed sky / Is not to walk in.
Good night then, Casca. This stormy sky is no weather to walk in.
Your ear is good. Cassius, what night is this!
You've got a good ear. Cassius, what a night this is!
A very pleasing night to honest men.
A very pleasant night for honest men.
Who ever knew the heavens menace so?
Whoever saw the heavens so threatening?

Those that have known the earth so full of faults. / For my part, I have walk'd about the streets, / Submitting me unto the perilous night; / And, thus unbraced, Casca, as you see, / Have bar'd my bosom to the thunder-stone; / And when the cross blue lightning seem'd to open / The breast of heaven, I did present myself / Even in the aim and very flash of it.

Those who have known the earth to be so full of wrongs. For my part, I have walked about the streets exposing myself to the dangerous night, and, with my shirt undone like this, Casca, as you see, I have bared my chest to the thunderbolts. And when the jagged blue lightning seemed to split open the sky, I put myself right where it was aimed, in its very flash.
But wherefore did you so much tempt the Heavens? / It is the part of men to fear and tremble, / When the most mighty gods by tokens send / Such dreadful heralds to astonish us.
But why did you tempt the heavens like that? It is right for men to fear and tremble when the mighty gods send such dreadful messengers as signs to terrify us.

You are dull, Casca; and those sparks of life / That should be in a Roman you do want, / Or else you use not. You look pale and gaze, / And put on fear and cast yourself in wonder, / To see the strange impatience of the Heavens: / But if you would consider the true cause / Why all these fires, why all these gliding ghosts, / Why birds and beasts, from quality and kind; / Why old men, fools, and children calculate, / Why all these things change from their ordinance, / Their natures, and pre-formed faculties, / To monstrous quality; why, you shall find / That Heaven hath infus'd them with these spirits, / To make them instruments of fear and warning / Unto some monstrous state. / Now could I, Casca, name to thee a man / Most like this dreadful night, / That thunders, lightens, opens graves, and roars, / As doth the lion in the Capitol; / A man no mightier than thyself, or me, / In personal action; yet prodigious grown, / And fearful, as these strange eruptions are.

You are slow, Casca, and you either lack the spark of life a Roman should have or you don't use it. You look pale and stare, and you are afraid and amazed to see the heavens so strangely angry. But if you thought about the real reason why there are all these fires, all these gliding ghosts, why birds and animals act against their nature, why old men, fools and children make prophecies, why all these things change from their normal ways and their natural abilities to become monstrous, you would find that heaven has filled them with these spirits to make them instruments of fear, warning of a monstrous state of affairs. Now, Casca, I could name a man to you who is very like this dreadful night, who thunders, flashes, opens graves and roars like the lion in the Capitol: a man no stronger than you or me in himself, and yet grown huge and frightening, like these strange outbreaks.
'Tis Caesar that you mean; is it not, Cassius?
It's Caesar you mean, isn't it, Cassius?

Let it be who it is: for Romans now / Have thews and limbs like to their ancestors; / But, woe the while! our fathers' minds are dead, / And we are govern'd with our mothers' spirits; / Our yoke and sufferance show us womanish.

Let it be whoever it is. Romans today have muscles and limbs like their ancestors, but, alas for our times, our fathers' minds are dead, and we are governed by our mothers' spirits. The way we put up with our yoke shows we are like women.
Indeed, they say the senators tomorrow / Mean to establish Caesar as a king; / And he shall wear his crown by sea and land, / In every place, save here in Italy.
In fact, they say the senators mean to make Caesar king tomorrow, and he will wear his crown on sea and land, everywhere except here in Italy.

I know where I will wear this dagger then; / Cassius from bondage will deliver Cassius: / Therein, ye gods, you make the weak most strong; / Therein, ye gods, you tyrants do defeat. / Nor stony tower, nor walls of beaten brass, / Nor airless dungeon, nor strong links of iron, / Can be retentive to the strength of spirit; / But life, being weary of these worldly bars, / Never lacks power to dismiss itself. / If I know this, know all the world besides, / That part of tyranny that I do bear / I can shake off at pleasure.

Then I know where I'll put this dagger: Cassius will free Cassius from slavery. That is how, you gods, you make the weak strongest; that is how, you gods, you defeat tyrants. No stone tower, no walls of hammered brass, no airless dungeon, no strong iron chains can imprison a determined spirit. Life, when it is tired of these earthly prison bars, always has the power to set itself free. If I know this, let the rest of the world know too: the share of tyranny I suffer I can throw off whenever I like.
So can I: / So every bondman in his own hand bears / The power to cancel his captivity.
So can I. Every slave holds in his own hand the power to end his captivity.

And why should Caesar be a tyrant then? / Poor man! I know he would not be a wolf, / But that he sees the Romans are but sheep: / He were no lion, were not Romans hinds. / Those that with haste will make a mighty fire / Begin it with weak straws. What trash is Rome, / What rubbish, and what offal, when it serves / For the base matter to illuminate / So vile a thing as Caesar! But, O grief, / Where hast thou led me? I, perhaps, speak this / Before a willing bondman: then I know / My answer must be made; but I am arm'd, / And dangers are to me indifferent.

Then why should Caesar be a tyrant? Poor man! I know he wouldn't be a wolf if he didn't see that the Romans are only sheep. He wouldn't be a lion if the Romans weren't deer. People who want to make a great fire in a hurry start it with feeble straws. What trash Rome is, what rubbish, what garbage, when it serves as the worthless fuel to light up something as vile as Caesar! But, oh grief, where have you led me? Perhaps I am saying this in front of a willing slave. Then I know I'll have to answer for it. But I am armed, and dangers mean nothing to me.
You speak to Casca, and to such a man / That is no fleering tell-tale. Hold, my hand: / Be factious for redress of all these griefs, / And I will set this foot of mine as far / As who goes farthest.
You are speaking to Casca, and he is no sneering tell-tale. Here, take my hand. Form a party to put right all these wrongs, and I will go as far as anyone goes.

There's a bargain made. / Now know you, Casca, I have mov'd already / Some certain of the noblest-minded Romans / To undergo with me an enterprise / Of honourable-dangerous consequence; / And I do know by this, they stay for me / In Pompey's Porch: for now, this fearful night, / There is no stir or walking in the streets; / And the complexion of the element / In favour's like the work we have in hand, / Most bloody, fiery, and most terrible.

That's a bargain. Now you should know, Casca, that I have already persuaded some of the noblest Romans to undertake with me an enterprise that is both honourable and dangerous. And I know that by now they are waiting for me in Pompey's Porch, because on this frightening night no one is moving or walking in the streets, and the look of the sky is like the work we have in hand: bloody, fiery and terrible.
Stand close awhile, for here comes one in haste.
Keep out of sight for a moment. Here comes someone in a hurry.
'Tis Cinna; I do know him by his gait; / He is a friend. Cinna, where haste you so?
It's Cinna. I know him by the way he walks. He's a friend. Cinna, where are you rushing to?
To find out you. Who's that? Metellus Cimber?
To find you. Who's that? Metellus Cimber?
No, it is Casca, one incorporate / To our attempts. Am I not stay'd for, Cinna?
No, it's Casca, who has joined our plans. Aren't they waiting for me, Cinna?
I am glad on't. What a fearful night is this! / There's two or three of us have seen strange sights.
I'm glad of it. What a frightening night this is! Two or three of us have seen strange sights.
Am I not stay'd for? tell me.
Aren't they waiting for me? Tell me.
Yes, you are. O Cassius, if you could / But win the noble Brutus to our party—
Yes, they are. Oh, Cassius, if you could only win noble Brutus over to our side—

Be you content. Good Cinna, take this paper, / And look you lay it in the praetor's chair, / Where Brutus may but find it; and throw this / In at his window; set this up with wax / Upon old Brutus' statue: all this done, / Repair to Pompey's Porch, where you shall find us. / Is Decius Brutus and Trebonius there?

Don't worry. Good Cinna, take this paper and make sure you put it on the judge's chair, where Brutus is sure to find it. Throw this one in at his window, and stick this one with wax on the statue of old Brutus. When all this is done, come back to Pompey's Porch, where you will find us. Are Decius Brutus and Trebonius there?
All but Metellus Cimber, and he's gone / To seek you at your house. Well, I will hie, / And so bestow these papers as you bade me.
Everyone except Metellus Cimber, and he's gone to look for you at your house. Well, I'll hurry and put these papers where you told me.
That done, repair to Pompey's theatre.
When that's done, come back to Pompey's theatre.
Come, Casca, you and I will yet, ere day, / See Brutus at his house: three parts of him / Is ours already, and the man entire / Upon the next encounter, yields him ours.
Come, Casca, you and I will go and see Brutus at his house before morning. Three quarters of him is ours already, and at the next meeting the whole man will give himself to us.
O, he sits high in all the people's hearts! / And that which would appear offence in us, / His countenance, like richest alchemy, / Will change to virtue and to worthiness.
Oh, he sits high in all the people's hearts! And what would look like a crime if we did it, his reputation, like the finest alchemy, will turn into virtue and worth.
Him, and his worth, and our great need of him, / You have right well conceited. Let us go, / For it is after midnight; and ere day, / We will awake him, and be sure of him.
You have understood very well how much he is worth and how much we need him. Let's go, because it's past midnight, and before dawn we will wake him and make sure of him.

What, Lucius, ho! / I cannot, by the progress of the stars, / Give guess how near to day.—Lucius, I say! / I would it were my fault to sleep so soundly. / When, Lucius, when? Awake, I say! What, Lucius!
Lucius! Hey! I can't tell from the position of the stars how close it is to morning. Lucius, I say! I wish I had the fault of sleeping so soundly. Come on, Lucius, come on! Wake up, I say! Lucius!
Get me a taper in my study, Lucius: / When it is lighted, come and call me here.
Put a candle in my study, Lucius. When it's lit, come and call me here.

It must be by his death: and for my part, / I know no personal cause to spurn at him, / But for the general. He would be crown'd: / How that might change his nature, there's the question. / It is the bright day that brings forth the adder, / And that craves wary walking. Crown him?—that; / And then, I grant, we put a sting in him, / That at his will he may do danger with. / Th' abuse of greatness is, when it disjoins / Remorse from power; and, to speak truth of Caesar, / I have not known when his affections sway'd / More than his reason. But 'tis a common proof, / That lowliness is young ambition's ladder, / Whereto the climber-upward turns his face; / But when he once attains the upmost round, / He then unto the ladder turns his back, / Looks in the clouds, scorning the base degrees / By which he did ascend. So Caesar may; / Then lest he may, prevent. And since the quarrel / Will bear no colour for the thing he is, / Fashion it thus: that what he is, augmented, / Would run to these and these extremities: / And therefore think him as a serpent's egg / Which hatch'd, would, as his kind grow mischievous; / And kill him in the shell.

It will have to be by his death. And for my own part, I have no personal reason to strike at him, only the good of the people. He wants to be crowned. How that might change his nature, that's the question. It's the bright sunshine that brings the snake out, and that calls for careful walking. Crown him? That's it. And then, I admit, we put a sting in him that he can use to do harm whenever he likes. Greatness is abused when it separates power from mercy. And to tell the truth about Caesar, I have never known his feelings rule his reason. But it's common experience that humility is the ladder young ambition climbs, with his face turned towards it as he goes up. But once he reaches the top rung, he turns his back on the ladder and looks into the clouds, scorning the lower steps he climbed by. Caesar might do that. So, in case he might, we must prevent it. And since our quarrel can't be justified by what he is now, put it like this: what he is, if increased, would run to these and these extremes. So think of him as a serpent's egg which, once hatched, would grow harmful like the rest of its kind, and kill him in the shell.
The taper burneth in your closet, sir. / Searching the window for a flint, I found / This paper, thus seal'd up, and I am sure / It did not lie there when I went to bed.
The candle is burning in your study, sir. While I was searching the window ledge for a flint, I found this paper, sealed like this, and I'm sure it wasn't there when I went to bed.
Get you to bed again; it is not day. / Is not tomorrow, boy, the Ides of March?
Go back to bed. It isn't day yet. Isn't tomorrow, boy, the fifteenth of March?
Look in the calendar, and bring me word.
Look in the calendar and tell me.
The exhalations, whizzing in the air / Give so much light that I may read by them.
The meteors whizzing through the air give so much light that I can read by them.

Brutus, thou sleep'st: awake and see thyself. / Shall Rome, &c. Speak, strike, redress! / "Brutus, thou sleep'st: awake!" / Such instigations have been often dropp'd / Where I have took them up. / "Shall Rome, &c." Thus must I piece it out: / Shall Rome stand under one man's awe? What, Rome? / My ancestors did from the streets of Rome / The Tarquin drive, when he was call'd a king. / "Speak, strike, redress!" Am I entreated / To speak and strike? O Rome, I make thee promise, / If the redress will follow, thou receivest / Thy full petition at the hand of Brutus.

"Brutus, you are asleep. Wake up and see yourself. Shall Rome, etc. Speak, strike, put things right!" "Brutus, you are asleep. Wake up!" Messages urging me like this have often been dropped where I have picked them up. "Shall Rome, etc." I must fill in the rest like this: shall Rome stand in awe of one man? What, Rome? My ancestors drove Tarquin out of the streets of Rome when he was called a king. "Speak, strike, put things right!" Am I being begged to speak and strike? Oh, Rome, I promise you, if putting things right will follow, you will get everything you ask for from the hand of Brutus.
Sir, March is wasted fifteen days.
Sir, fifteen days of March have passed.
'Tis good. Go to the gate, somebody knocks.
Good. Go to the gate, someone is knocking.

Since Cassius first did whet me against Caesar, / I have not slept. / Between the acting of a dreadful thing / And the first motion, all the interim is / Like a phantasma, or a hideous dream: / The genius and the mortal instruments / Are then in council; and the state of man, / Like to a little kingdom, suffers then / The nature of an insurrection.

Since Cassius first sharpened me against Caesar, I haven't slept. Between doing a dreadful thing and first thinking of it, all the time in between is like a nightmare or a hideous dream. The mind and the body's powers are then arguing it out, and a man, like a little kingdom, goes through a kind of rebellion.
Sir, 'tis your brother Cassius at the door, / Who doth desire to see you.
Sir, it's your brother-in-law Cassius at the door, and he wants to see you.
No, sir, there are moe with him.
No, sir, there are more with him.
No, sir, their hats are pluck'd about their ears, / And half their faces buried in their cloaks, / That by no means I may discover them / By any mark of favour.
No, sir. Their hats are pulled down over their ears, and half their faces are buried in their cloaks, so that I can't make them out by any feature at all.

They are the faction. O conspiracy, / Sham'st thou to show thy dangerous brow by night, / When evils are most free? O, then, by day / Where wilt thou find a cavern dark enough / To mask thy monstrous visage? Seek none, conspiracy; / Hide it in smiles and affability: / For if thou path, thy native semblance on, / Not Erebus itself were dim enough / To hide thee from prevention.

They are the conspirators. Oh, conspiracy, are you ashamed to show your dangerous face even at night, when evil is most free? Oh, then, by day where will you find a cave dark enough to hide your monstrous face? Don't look for one, conspiracy. Hide it in smiles and friendliness. Because if you walk about in your true appearance, not even the darkness of the underworld would be dark enough to keep you from being stopped.
I think we are too bold upon your rest: / Good morrow, Brutus; do we trouble you?
I think we are disturbing your rest too boldly. Good morning, Brutus. Are we troubling you?
I have been up this hour, awake all night. / Know I these men that come along with you?
I've been up this past hour, awake all night. Do I know these men who have come with you?
Yes, every man of them; and no man here / But honours you; and everyone doth wish / You had but that opinion of yourself / Which every noble Roman bears of you. / This is Trebonius.
Yes, every one of them. And there is no man here who doesn't honour you, and every one wishes you had the opinion of yourself that every noble Roman has of you. This is Trebonius.
This, Casca; this, Cinna; and this, Metellus Cimber.
This is Casca; this is Cinna; and this is Metellus Cimber.
They are all welcome. / What watchful cares do interpose themselves / Betwixt your eyes and night?
They are all welcome. What cares keep you awake and come between your eyes and the night?
May I have a word with you?
Here lies the east: doth not the day break here?
This is east. Isn't the day breaking here?
O, pardon, sir, it doth; and yon grey lines / That fret the clouds are messengers of day.
Oh, excuse me, sir, it is. And those grey streaks lining the clouds over there are messengers of the day.

You shall confess that you are both deceiv'd. / Here, as I point my sword, the Sun arises; / Which is a great way growing on the South, / Weighing the youthful season of the year. / Some two months hence, up higher toward the North / He first presents his fire; and the high East / Stands, as the Capitol, directly here.

You'll have to admit you're both wrong. The sun rises here, where I'm pointing my sword, a long way to the south, considering it's still early in the year. In about two months it will first appear higher up towards the north, and due east is here, in line with the Capitol.
Give me your hands all over, one by one.
Give me your hands, all of you, one by one.
And let us swear our resolution.
And let's swear an oath to our decision.

No, not an oath. If not the face of men, / The sufferance of our souls, the time's abuse— / If these be motives weak, break off betimes, / And every man hence to his idle bed. / So let high-sighted tyranny range on, / Till each man drop by lottery. But if these, / As I am sure they do, bear fire enough / To kindle cowards, and to steel with valour / The melting spirits of women; then, countrymen, / What need we any spur but our own cause / To prick us to redress? what other bond / Than secret Romans, that have spoke the word, / And will not palter? and what other oath / Than honesty to honesty engag'd, / That this shall be, or we will fall for it? / Swear priests and cowards, and men cautelous, / Old feeble carrions, and such suffering souls / That welcome wrongs; unto bad causes swear / Such creatures as men doubt; but do not stain / The even virtue of our enterprise, / Nor th' insuppressive mettle of our spirits, / To think that or our cause or our performance / Did need an oath; when every drop of blood / That every Roman bears, and nobly bears, / Is guilty of a several bastardy, / If he do break the smallest particle / Of any promise that hath pass'd from him.

No, not an oath. If the look on men's faces, the suffering of our souls and the corruption of the times are weak motives, let's give up now and every man go back to his lazy bed. Then let ambitious tyranny run wild until each of us dies at the tyrant's whim. But if these motives, as I am sure they do, have fire enough to set cowards alight and to harden with courage the soft spirits of women, then, countrymen, what spur do we need but our own cause to drive us to put things right? What other bond than that we are Romans who can keep a secret, who have given our word and won't go back on it? And what other oath than honest men pledged to each other that this will happen or we will die for it? Let priests and cowards and cautious men swear, and feeble old wrecks and those meek souls who welcome being wronged. Let creatures that no one trusts swear to bad causes. But don't stain the pure virtue of our enterprise or the unconquerable courage of our spirits by thinking that either our cause or our action needs an oath, when every drop of blood in every Roman, nobly carried, would prove itself not truly his, if he broke the smallest part of any promise he had made.
But what of Cicero? Shall we sound him? / I think he will stand very strong with us.
But what about Cicero? Shall we sound him out? I think he will stand firmly with us.
Let us not leave him out.

O, let us have him, for his silver hairs / Will purchase us a good opinion, / And buy men's voices to commend our deeds. / It shall be said, his judgement rul'd our hands; / Our youths and wildness shall no whit appear, / But all be buried in his gravity.

Oh, let's have him, because his silver hair will win us a good reputation and buy men's voices to praise what we do. People will say his judgement guided our hands. Our youth and wildness won't show at all, but will be buried under his seriousness.
O, name him not; let us not break with him; / For he will never follow anything / That other men begin.
Oh, don't mention him. Let's not tell him our plans, because he will never follow anything that other men have started.
Shall no man else be touch'd but only Caesar?
Is no one else to be touched except Caesar?

Decius, well urg'd. I think it is not meet, / Mark Antony, so well belov'd of Caesar, / Should outlive Caesar: we shall find of him / A shrewd contriver; and you know, his means, / If he improve them, may well stretch so far / As to annoy us all; which to prevent, / Let Antony and Caesar fall together.

Decius, good point. I don't think it's right that Mark Antony, whom Caesar loves so much, should outlive Caesar. We'll find him a cunning schemer. And you know his resources, if he makes the most of them, could stretch far enough to harm us all. To prevent that, let Antony and Caesar fall together.

Our course will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius, / To cut the head off, and then hack the limbs, / Like wrath in death, and envy afterwards; / For Antony is but a limb of Caesar. / Let us be sacrificers, but not butchers, Caius. / We all stand up against the spirit of Caesar, / And in the spirit of men there is no blood. / O, that we then could come by Caesar's spirit, / And not dismember Caesar! But, alas, / Caesar must bleed for it! And, gentle friends, / Let's kill him boldly, but not wrathfully; / Let's carve him as a dish fit for the gods, / Not hew him as a carcass fit for hounds. / And let our hearts, as subtle masters do, / Stir up their servants to an act of rage, / And after seem to chide 'em. This shall mark / Our purpose necessary, and not envious; / Which so appearing to the common eyes, / We shall be call'd purgers, not murderers. / And for Mark Antony, think not of him; / For he can do no more than Caesar's arm / When Caesar's head is off.

Our action will seem too bloody, Caius Cassius, to cut the head off and then hack at the limbs, as if we killed in anger and kept up the hatred afterwards, because Antony is only a limb of Caesar. Let us be sacrificers, not butchers, Caius. We are all standing up against the spirit of Caesar, and in men's spirits there is no blood. Oh, if only we could get at Caesar's spirit and not cut up Caesar! But, alas, Caesar must bleed for it. And, gentle friends, let's kill him boldly but not angrily. Let's carve him like a dish fit for the gods, not hack him like a carcass fit for dogs. And let our hearts, like cunning masters, stir up their servants, our hands, to a violent act, and then seem to scold them for it. This will make our purpose look necessary and not spiteful. And if it looks like that to ordinary people, we'll be called healers who purge the state, not murderers. As for Mark Antony, don't think about him, because he can do no more than Caesar's arm can once Caesar's head is off.
Yet I fear him; / For in the ingrafted love he bears to Caesar—
Still, I fear him, because of the deep-rooted love he has for Caesar—

Alas, good Cassius, do not think of him: / If he love Caesar, all that he can do / Is to himself; take thought and die for Caesar. / And that were much he should; for he is given / To sports, to wildness, and much company.

Oh, good Cassius, don't think about him. If he loves Caesar, all he can do is harm himself: grieve and die for Caesar. And that would be a lot to expect of him, because he loves sport, wild living and plenty of company.
There is no fear in him; let him not die; / For he will live, and laugh at this hereafter.
There's nothing to fear in him. Don't let him die, because he'll live and laugh about this afterwards.
Quiet! Count the strokes of the clock.

But it is doubtful yet / Whether Caesar will come forth today or no; / For he is superstitious grown of late, / Quite from the main opinion he held once / Of fantasy, of dreams, and ceremonies. / It may be these apparent prodigies, / The unaccustom'd terror of this night, / And the persuasion of his augurers, / May hold him from the Capitol today.

But it's still uncertain whether Caesar will come out today or not, because he has grown superstitious lately, quite unlike the strong opinion he once held about fancies, dreams and omens. It may be that these obvious signs, the unusual terrors of this night and the persuasion of his fortune-tellers will keep him away from the Capitol today.

Never fear that: if he be so resolved, / I can o'ersway him, for he loves to hear / That unicorns may be betray'd with trees, / And bears with glasses, elephants with holes, / Lions with toils, and men with flatterers. / But when I tell him he hates flatterers, / He says he does, being then most flattered. / Let me work; / For I can give his humour the true bent, / And I will bring him to the Capitol.

Don't worry about that. If he has made up his mind to stay, I can win him round, because he loves to hear that unicorns can be trapped by trees, bears with mirrors, elephants with pits, lions with nets, and men with flatterers. But when I tell him he hates flatterers, he says he does, and that's when he is most flattered. Let me work on him, because I can turn his mood the right way, and I will bring him to the Capitol.
Nay, we will all of us be there to fetch him.
No, we'll all be there to fetch him.
By the eighth hour: is that the uttermost?
By eight o'clock. Is that the latest?
Be that the uttermost; and fail not then.
Let that be the latest, and don't fail to be there.
Caius Ligarius doth bear Caesar hard, / Who rated him for speaking well of Pompey; / I wonder none of you have thought of him.
Caius Ligarius has a grudge against Caesar, who told him off for speaking well of Pompey. I'm surprised none of you have thought of him.
Now, good Metellus, go along by him: / He loves me well, and I have given him reason; / Send him but hither, and I'll fashion him.
Now, good Metellus, go to his house. He loves me, and I have given him reason to. Just send him here and I'll shape him to our purpose.
The morning comes upon's. We'll leave you, Brutus. / And, friends, disperse yourselves; but all remember / What you have said, and show yourselves true Romans.
Morning is coming on us. We'll leave you, Brutus. And, friends, go your separate ways, but all of you remember what you have said and show yourselves true Romans.

Good gentlemen, look fresh and merrily; / Let not our looks put on our purposes, / But bear it as our Roman actors do, / With untired spirits and formal constancy. / And so, good morrow to you everyone.

Good gentlemen, look fresh and cheerful. Don't let our faces show what we intend, but carry it off as our Roman actors do, with tireless spirits and steady composure. And so, good morning to every one of you.

Boy! Lucius! Fast asleep? It is no matter; / Enjoy the honey-heavy dew of slumber: / Thou hast no figures nor no fantasies, / Which busy care draws in the brains of men; / Therefore thou sleep'st so sound.
Boy! Lucius! Fast asleep? It doesn't matter. Enjoy the sweet, heavy dew of sleep. You have no imaginings or fantasies that busy worry draws in men's minds, and that's why you sleep so soundly.
Portia, what mean you? Wherefore rise you now? / It is not for your health thus to commit / Your weak condition to the raw cold morning.
Portia, what are you doing? Why are you up now? It isn't good for your health to expose your delicate body to the raw, cold morning.

Nor for yours neither. Y' have ungently, Brutus, / Stole from my bed; and yesternight at supper, / You suddenly arose, and walk'd about, / Musing and sighing, with your arms across; / And when I ask'd you what the matter was, / You star'd upon me with ungentle looks. / I urg'd you further; then you scratch'd your head, / And too impatiently stamp'd with your foot; / Yet I insisted, yet you answer'd not, / But with an angry wafture of your hand / Gave sign for me to leave you. So I did, / Fearing to strengthen that impatience / Which seem'd too much enkindled; and withal / Hoping it was but an effect of humour, / Which sometime hath his hour with every man. / It will not let you eat, nor talk, nor sleep; / And could it work so much upon your shape / As it hath much prevail'd on your condition, / I should not know you, Brutus. Dear my lord, / Make me acquainted with your cause of grief.

Nor for yours either. You crept unkindly from my bed, Brutus. And last night at supper you suddenly got up and walked about, brooding and sighing, with your arms folded. And when I asked you what was wrong, you stared at me unkindly. I pressed you further; then you scratched your head and stamped your foot too impatiently. Still I insisted, and still you didn't answer, but with an angry wave of your hand signalled me to leave you. So I did, afraid of making worse an impatience that seemed already too inflamed, and hoping too that it was only a passing mood, which every man has sometimes. It won't let you eat or talk or sleep, and if it could change your appearance as much as it has changed your temper, I wouldn't recognise you, Brutus. My dear lord, tell me the cause of your unhappiness.
I am not well in health, and that is all.
I am not well, and that's all.
Brutus is wise, and, were he not in health, / He would embrace the means to come by it.
Brutus is wise, and if he weren't well he would do what he needed to get better.
Why, so I do. Good Portia, go to bed.
Why, so I am. Good Portia, go to bed.

Is Brutus sick, and is it physical / To walk unbraced and suck up the humours / Of the dank morning? What, is Brutus sick, / And will he steal out of his wholesome bed / To dare the vile contagion of the night, / And tempt the rheumy and unpurged air / To add unto his sickness? No, my Brutus; / You have some sick offence within your mind, / Which, by the right and virtue of my place, / I ought to know of: and, upon my knees, / I charm you, by my once commended beauty, / By all your vows of love, and that great vow / Which did incorporate and make us one, / That you unfold to me, your self, your half, / Why you are heavy, and what men tonight / Have had resort to you; for here have been / Some six or seven, who did hide their faces / Even from darkness.

Is Brutus sick, and is it healthy to walk about with his clothes undone, breathing in the damp morning air? What, is Brutus sick, and will he creep out of his healthy bed to risk the foul diseases of the night and tempt the damp, unclean air to make him sicker? No, my Brutus, you have some illness in your mind, which I have a right, as your wife, to know about. And on my knees I beg you, by my beauty which you once praised, by all your vows of love, and by that great vow which joined us into one, that you reveal to me, your self, your other half, why you are so sad, and what men have visited you tonight. Six or seven have been here, who hid their faces even from the darkness.

I should not need, if you were gentle Brutus. / Within the bond of marriage, tell me, Brutus, / Is it excepted I should know no secrets / That appertain to you? Am I your self / But, as it were, in sort or limitation, / To keep with you at meals, comfort your bed, / And talk to you sometimes? Dwell I but in the suburbs / Of your good pleasure? If it be no more, / Portia is Brutus' harlot, not his wife.

I wouldn't need to if you were gentle Brutus. Tell me, Brutus, is it a condition of our marriage that I shouldn't know any secrets that concern you? Am I part of you only in a limited way, to keep you company at meals, comfort you in bed and talk to you sometimes? Do I live only on the outskirts of your affection? If that's all, Portia is Brutus's whore, not his wife.
You are my true and honourable wife, / As dear to me as are the ruddy drops / That visit my sad heart.
You are my true and honourable wife, as dear to me as the red drops of blood that flow through my sad heart.

If this were true, then should I know this secret. / I grant I am a woman; but withal / A woman that Lord Brutus took to wife; / I grant I am a woman; but withal / A woman well reputed, Cato's daughter. / Think you I am no stronger than my sex, / Being so father'd and so husbanded? / Tell me your counsels, I will not disclose 'em. / I have made strong proof of my constancy, / Giving myself a voluntary wound / Here, in the thigh: can I bear that with patience / And not my husband's secrets?

If that were true, I would know this secret. I admit I am a woman, but a woman whom Lord Brutus took as his wife. I admit I am a woman, but a woman with a good name, Cato's daughter. Do you think I am no stronger than other women, with such a father and such a husband? Tell me your plans; I won't reveal them. I have given strong proof of my firmness by deliberately wounding myself here, in the thigh. Can I bear that patiently and not my husband's secrets?
O ye gods, / Render me worthy of this noble wife!
Oh, you gods, make me worthy of this noble wife!

Hark, hark, one knocks. Portia, go in awhile; / And by and by thy bosom shall partake / The secrets of my heart. / All my engagements I will construe to thee, / All the charactery of my sad brows. / Leave me with haste.

Listen, listen, someone is knocking. Portia, go inside for a while, and soon your heart will share the secrets of mine. I will explain all my commitments to you, and everything written in my sad face. Leave me, quickly.
Here is a sick man that would speak with you.
Here's a sick man who wants to speak to you.
Caius Ligarius, that Metellus spake of. / Boy, stand aside. Caius Ligarius, how?
It's Caius Ligarius, the one Metellus talked about. Boy, stand aside. Caius Ligarius, how are you?
Vouchsafe good-morrow from a feeble tongue.
Accept a good morning from a weak voice.
O, what a time have you chose out, brave Caius, / To wear a kerchief! Would you were not sick!
Oh, what a time you have chosen, brave Caius, to wear a sick man's scarf! I wish you weren't ill!
I am not sick, if Brutus have in hand / Any exploit worthy the name of honour.
I'm not ill, if Brutus has in hand any deed worthy to be called honourable.
Such an exploit have I in hand, Ligarius, / Had you a healthful ear to hear of it.
I have such a deed in hand, Ligarius, if you had a healthy ear to hear about it.

By all the gods that Romans bow before, / I here discard my sickness. Soul of Rome! / Brave son, derived from honourable loins! / Thou, like an exorcist, hast conjur'd up / My mortified spirit. Now bid me run, / And I will strive with things impossible, / Yea, get the better of them. What's to do?

By all the gods that Romans bow to, I throw off my sickness now. Soul of Rome! Brave son, born of an honourable family! Like a magician, you have called up my deadened spirit. Now tell me to run and I will struggle with impossible things, yes, and beat them. What is to be done?
A piece of work that will make sick men whole.
A piece of work that will make sick men well.
But are not some whole that we must make sick?
But aren't there some well men we must make sick?
That must we also. What it is, my Caius, / I shall unfold to thee, as we are going, / To whom it must be done.
We must do that too. What it is, my Caius, and who it must be done to, I'll explain to you as we walk.
Set on your foot, / And with a heart new-fir'd I follow you, / To do I know not what; but it sufficeth / That Brutus leads me on.
Lead on, and with a heart set on fire again I'll follow you to do I don't know what. It's enough that Brutus leads me.
Nor heaven nor earth have been at peace tonight: / Thrice hath Calphurnia in her sleep cried out, / "Help, ho! They murder Caesar!" Who's within?
Neither heaven nor earth has been at peace tonight. Three times Calphurnia has cried out in her sleep, "Help! They are murdering Caesar!" Who's there?
Go bid the priests do present sacrifice, / And bring me their opinions of success.
Go and tell the priests to make a sacrifice at once, and bring me their opinion of how things will go.
What mean you, Caesar? Think you to walk forth? / You shall not stir out of your house today.
What are you doing, Caesar? Are you thinking of going out? You shall not set foot out of the house today.
Caesar shall forth. The things that threaten'd me / Ne'er look'd but on my back; when they shall see / The face of Caesar, they are vanished.
Caesar will go out. The things that threatened me have only ever seen my back. When they see Caesar's face, they vanish.

Caesar, I never stood on ceremonies, / Yet now they fright me. There is one within, / Besides the things that we have heard and seen, / Recounts most horrid sights seen by the watch. / A lioness hath whelped in the streets, / And graves have yawn'd, and yielded up their dead; / Fierce fiery warriors fight upon the clouds / In ranks and squadrons and right form of war, / Which drizzled blood upon the Capitol; / The noise of battle hurtled in the air, / Horses did neigh, and dying men did groan, / And ghosts did shriek and squeal about the streets. / O Caesar, these things are beyond all use, / And I do fear them!

Caesar, I never paid attention to omens, but now they frighten me. There is someone in the house who, besides the things we have heard and seen, tells of the most horrible sights seen by the night watch. A lioness has given birth in the streets, and graves have opened and given up their dead. Fierce, fiery warriors fight on the clouds in ranks and squadrons and proper battle formation, and they drizzled blood on the Capitol. The noise of battle clashed in the air, horses neighed, dying men groaned, and ghosts shrieked and squealed in the streets. Oh, Caesar, these things are beyond all experience, and I'm afraid of them!
What can be avoided / Whose end is purpos'd by the mighty gods? / Yet Caesar shall go forth; for these predictions / Are to the world in general as to Caesar.
What can be avoided if the mighty gods have decided it? Still, Caesar will go out, because these predictions apply to the world in general as much as to Caesar.
When beggars die, there are no comets seen; / The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.
When beggars die, no comets are seen. The heavens themselves blaze out the death of princes.

Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once. / Of all the wonders that I yet have heard, / It seems to me most strange that men should fear, / Seeing that death, a necessary end, / Will come when it will come.

Cowards die many times before they actually die. The brave only taste death once. Of all the wonders I have heard of, the strangest to me is that men should be afraid, since death, which no one can escape, will come when it will come.
They would not have you to stir forth today. / Plucking the entrails of an offering forth, / They could not find a heart within the beast.
They don't want you to go out today. When they pulled out the insides of the sacrificed animal, they couldn't find a heart in the beast.

The gods do this in shame of cowardice: / Caesar should be a beast without a heart / If he should stay at home today for fear. / No, Caesar shall not. Danger knows full well / That Caesar is more dangerous than he. / We are two lions litter'd in one day, / And I the elder and more terrible, / And Caesar shall go forth.

The gods do this to shame cowardice. Caesar would be a beast without a heart if he stayed at home today out of fear. No, Caesar will not. Danger knows very well that Caesar is more dangerous than he is. We are two lions born on the same day, and I am the elder and more terrible. And Caesar will go out.

Alas, my lord, / Your wisdom is consum'd in confidence. / Do not go forth today: call it my fear / That keeps you in the house, and not your own. / We'll send Mark Antony to the Senate-house, / And he shall say you are not well today. / Let me upon my knee prevail in this.

Oh, my lord, your wisdom is eaten up by overconfidence. Don't go out today. Say it's my fear that keeps you in the house, not your own. We'll send Mark Antony to the Senate house, and he will say you aren't well today. On my knees, let me win this.
Mark Antony shall say I am not well, / And for thy humour, I will stay at home.
Mark Antony will say I'm not well, and to please you I'll stay at home.
Here's Decius Brutus, he shall tell them so.
Here's Decius Brutus. He'll tell them so.
Caesar, all hail! Good morrow, worthy Caesar. / I come to fetch you to the Senate-house.
Hail, Caesar! Good morning, worthy Caesar. I've come to bring you to the Senate house.

And you are come in very happy time / To bear my greeting to the Senators, / And tell them that I will not come today. / Cannot, is false; and that I dare not, falser: / I will not come today. Tell them so, Decius.

And you have come at just the right time to take my greetings to the senators and tell them I won't come today. That I cannot is false, and that I dare not is falser. I will not come today. Tell them that, Decius.
Shall Caesar send a lie? / Have I in conquest stretch'd mine arm so far, / To be afeard to tell grey-beards the truth? / Decius, go tell them Caesar will not come.
Shall Caesar send a lie? Have I stretched my arm so far in conquest only to be afraid of telling the truth to some old greybeards? Decius, go and tell them Caesar will not come.
Most mighty Caesar, let me know some cause, / Lest I be laugh'd at when I tell them so.
