Most mighty Caesar, give me some reason, so that I'm not laughed at when I tell them.

The cause is in my will; I will not come. / That is enough to satisfy the Senate. / But for your private satisfaction, / Because I love you, I will let you know: / Calphurnia here, my wife, stays me at home. / She dreamt tonight she saw my statue, / Which like a fountain with an hundred spouts / Did run pure blood; and many lusty Romans / Came smiling, and did bathe their hands in it. / And these does she apply for warnings and portents / And evils imminent; and on her knee / Hath begg'd that I will stay at home today.

The reason is my will: I will not come. That is enough to satisfy the Senate. But for your private satisfaction, because I love you, I'll tell you. Calphurnia here, my wife, is keeping me at home. Last night she dreamt she saw my statue, which ran with pure blood like a fountain with a hundred spouts, and many strong, cheerful Romans came smiling and bathed their hands in it. She interprets these as warnings and omens of evils about to happen, and on her knees she has begged me to stay at home today.

This dream is all amiss interpreted: / It was a vision fair and fortunate. / Your statue spouting blood in many pipes, / In which so many smiling Romans bath'd, / Signifies that from you great Rome shall suck / Reviving blood, and that great men shall press / For tinctures, stains, relics, and cognizance. / This by Calphurnia's dream is signified.

This dream has been completely misinterpreted. It was a fair and lucky vision. Your statue spouting blood from many pipes, in which so many smiling Romans bathed, means that great Rome will suck reviving blood from you, and that great men will crowd round for cloths dipped in it, for stains, relics and badges to remember you by. That is what Calphurnia's dream means.
And this way have you well expounded it.
And you have explained it well that way.

I have, when you have heard what I can say; / And know it now. The Senate have concluded / To give this day a crown to mighty Caesar. / If you shall send them word you will not come, / Their minds may change. Besides, it were a mock / Apt to be render'd, for someone to say, / "Break up the Senate till another time, / When Caesar's wife shall meet with better dreams." / If Caesar hide himself, shall they not whisper / "Lo, Caesar is afraid"? / Pardon me, Caesar; for my dear dear love / To your proceeding bids me tell you this, / And reason to my love is liable.

I have, as you'll see when you've heard what I have to say. And know this now: the Senate has decided to give a crown to mighty Caesar today. If you send word that you won't come, they may change their minds. Besides, someone would be likely to make a joke of it and say, "Close the Senate until another time, when Caesar's wife has better dreams." If Caesar hides, won't they whisper, "Look, Caesar is afraid"? Forgive me, Caesar, because my deep, deep love for your advancement makes me tell you this, and my love overrules my sense of what is proper.
How foolish do your fears seem now, Calphurnia! / I am ashamed I did yield to them. / Give me my robe, for I will go.
How foolish your fears seem now, Calphurnia! I'm ashamed I gave in to them. Give me my robe, because I will go.
And look where Publius is come to fetch me.
And look, here's Publius come to fetch me.

Welcome, Publius. / What, Brutus, are you stirr'd so early too? / Good morrow, Casca. Caius Ligarius, / Caesar was ne'er so much your enemy / As that same ague which hath made you lean. / What is't o'clock?
Welcome, Publius. What, Brutus, are you up so early too? Good morning, Casca. Caius Ligarius, Caesar was never as much your enemy as that fever which has made you so thin. What time is it?
I thank you for your pains and courtesy.
Thank you for your trouble and courtesy.
See! Antony, that revels long a-nights, / Is notwithstanding up. Good morrow, Antony.
Look! Antony, who stays up partying late at night, is up all the same. Good morning, Antony.
And to you, most noble Caesar.

Bid them prepare within. / I am to blame to be thus waited for. / Now, Cinna; now, Metellus; what, Trebonius! / I have an hour's talk in store for you: / Remember that you call on me today; / Be near me, that I may remember you.

Tell them to get ready inside. I am at fault for keeping you waiting like this. Now, Cinna; now, Metellus; what, Trebonius! I have an hour's talk saved up for you. Remember to come and see me today. Stay near me so that I remember you.
Caesar, I will. [Aside] and so near will I be, / That your best friends shall wish I had been further.
Caesar, I will. [Aside] And I'll be so near that your best friends will wish I had been further away.
Good friends, go in, and taste some wine with me; / And we, like friends, will straightway go together.
Good friends, come in and have some wine with me, and then, like friends, we'll go along together at once.
[Aside] That every like is not the same, O Caesar, / The heart of Brutus yearns to think upon.
[Aside] Brutus's heart aches to think that being like friends is not the same as being friends, Caesar.

"Caesar, beware of Brutus; take heed of Cassius; come not near Casca; / have an eye to Cinna; trust not Trebonius; mark well Metellus Cimber; / Decius Brutus loves thee not; thou hast wrong'd Caius Ligarius. There / is but one mind in all these men, and it is bent against Caesar. If / thou be'st not immortal, look about you: security gives way to / conspiracy. The mighty gods defend thee! / Thy lover, Artemidorus." / Here will I stand till Caesar pass along, / And as a suitor will I give him this. / My heart laments that virtue cannot live / Out of the teeth of emulation. / If thou read this, O Caesar, thou mayest live; / If not, the Fates with traitors do contrive.

"Caesar, beware of Brutus; watch out for Cassius; don't go near Casca; keep an eye on Cinna; don't trust Trebonius; watch Metellus Cimber closely; Decius Brutus doesn't love you; you have wronged Caius Ligarius. All these men have one purpose, and it is aimed at Caesar. If you are not immortal, look about you: overconfidence opens the way to conspiracy. May the mighty gods defend you! Your friend, Artemidorus." I'll stand here until Caesar passes, and give him this as if it were a petition. My heart grieves that goodness cannot live beyond the reach of envy's teeth. If you read this, Caesar, you may live. If not, the Fates are plotting with the traitors.
I pr'ythee, boy, run to the Senate-house; / Stay not to answer me, but get thee gone. / Why dost thou stay?
Please, boy, run to the Senate house. Don't stop to answer me, just go. Why are you waiting?
To find out what I'm to do there, madam.

I would have had thee there and here again, / Ere I can tell thee what thou shouldst do there. / [Aside] O constancy, be strong upon my side, / Set a huge mountain 'tween my heart and tongue! / I have a man's mind, but a woman's might. / How hard it is for women to keep counsel! / Art thou here yet?

I'd have liked you to be there and back again before I could tell you what to do there. [Aside] Oh, self-control, stay firmly on my side, and put a huge mountain between my heart and my tongue! I have a man's mind but a woman's strength. How hard it is for women to keep a secret! Are you still here?
Madam, what should I do? / Run to the Capitol, and nothing else? / And so return to you, and nothing else?
Madam, what should I do? Run to the Capitol, and nothing else? And then come back to you, and nothing else?
Yes, bring me word, boy, if thy lord look well, / For he went sickly forth: and take good note / What Caesar doth, what suitors press to him. / Hark, boy, what noise is that?

Yes, come back and tell me, boy, if your master looks well, because he was unwell when he went out. And take careful note of what Caesar does, and which petitioners crowd round him. Listen, boy, what's that noise?
Pr'ythee, listen well. / I heard a bustling rumour, like a fray, / And the wind brings it from the Capitol.
Please, listen carefully. I heard a confused noise, like a fight, and the wind is bringing it from the Capitol.
Honestly, madam, I can't hear anything.
Come hither, fellow: / Which way hast thou been?
Come here, fellow. Where have you come from?
At mine own house, good lady.
From my own house, good lady.
Is Caesar yet gone to the Capitol?
Has Caesar gone to the Capitol yet?
Madam, not yet. I go to take my stand, / To see him pass on to the Capitol.
Not yet, madam. I'm going to find a place to watch him go by on his way to the Capitol.
Thou hast some suit to Caesar, hast thou not?
You have a petition for Caesar, don't you?
That I have, lady, if it will please Caesar / To be so good to Caesar as to hear me, / I shall beseech him to befriend himself.
I have, lady. If Caesar will be good enough to himself to listen to me, I will beg him to look after himself.
Why, know'st thou any harm's intended towards him?
Why, do you know of any harm intended against him?

None that I know will be, much that I fear may chance. / Good morrow to you. Here the street is narrow. / The throng that follows Caesar at the heels, / Of Senators, of Praetors, common suitors, / Will crowd a feeble man almost to death: / I'll get me to a place more void, and there / Speak to great Caesar as he comes along.

None that I know will happen, but much that I fear may. Good morning to you. The street is narrow here. The crowd of senators, magistrates and ordinary petitioners at Caesar's heels will squeeze a weak man almost to death. I'll find a less crowded place and speak to great Caesar there as he comes by.

I must go in. / [Aside] Ay me, how weak a thing / The heart of woman is! O Brutus, / The heavens speed thee in thine enterprise! / Sure, the boy heard me. Brutus hath a suit / That Caesar will not grant. O, I grow faint. / Run, Lucius, and commend me to my lord; / Say I am merry; come to me again, / And bring me word what he doth say to thee.

I must go in. [Aside] Oh dear, what a weak thing a woman's heart is! Oh, Brutus, may the heavens help you in your enterprise! I'm sure the boy heard me. Brutus has a petition that Caesar won't grant. Oh, I feel faint. Run, Lucius, and give my love to my husband. Tell him I'm cheerful, then come back to me and tell me what he says to you.
The Ides of March are come.
The fifteenth of March has come.
Yes, Caesar, but it hasn't gone.
Trebonius doth desire you to o'er-read, / At your best leisure, this his humble suit.
Trebonius asks you to read through his humble petition when you have time.
O Caesar, read mine first; for mine's a suit / That touches Caesar nearer. Read it, great Caesar.
Oh, Caesar, read mine first, because my petition concerns Caesar more closely. Read it, great Caesar.
What touches us ourself shall be last serv'd.
What concerns me personally will be dealt with last.
Delay not, Caesar. Read it instantly.
Don't delay, Caesar. Read it at once.
You there, get out of the way.
What, urge you your petitions in the street? / Come to the Capitol.
What, are you pushing your petitions in the street? Come to the Capitol.
I wish your enterprise today may thrive.
I hope your enterprise succeeds today.
He wish'd today our enterprise might thrive. / I fear our purpose is discovered.
He hoped our enterprise would succeed today. I'm afraid our plan has been discovered.
Look how he makes to Caesar: mark him.
Look how he's going up to Caesar. Watch him.
Casca, be sudden, for we fear prevention. / Brutus, what shall be done? If this be known, / Cassius or Caesar never shall turn back, / For I will slay myself.
Casca, be quick, because we're afraid of being stopped. Brutus, what shall we do? If this is known, either Cassius or Caesar will never go home, because I'll kill myself.
Cassius, be constant: / Popilius Lena speaks not of our purposes; / For look, he smiles, and Caesar doth not change.
Cassius, stay calm. Popilius Lena isn't talking about our plans. Look, he's smiling, and Caesar's face doesn't change.
Trebonius knows his time, for look you, Brutus, / He draws Mark Antony out of the way.
Trebonius knows his moment. Look, Brutus, he's drawing Mark Antony out of the way.
Where is Metellus Cimber? Let him go, / And presently prefer his suit to Caesar.
Where is Metellus Cimber? Let him go and present his petition to Caesar now.
He is address'd; press near and second him.
He's ready. Move in close and back him up.
Casca, you are the first that rears your hand.
Casca, you are the first to raise your hand.
Are we all ready? What is now amiss / That Caesar and his Senate must redress?
Are we all ready? What is wrong now that Caesar and his Senate must put right?
Most high, most mighty, and most puissant Caesar, / Metellus Cimber throws before thy seat / An humble heart.
Most high, most mighty and most powerful Caesar, Metellus Cimber throws down a humble heart before your seat.

I must prevent thee, Cimber. / These couchings and these lowly courtesies / Might fire the blood of ordinary men, / And turn pre-ordinance and first decree / Into the law of children. Be not fond, / To think that Caesar bears such rebel blood / That will be thaw'd from the true quality / With that which melteth fools; I mean sweet words, / Low-crooked curtsies, and base spaniel fawning. / Thy brother by decree is banished: / If thou dost bend, and pray, and fawn for him, / I spurn thee like a cur out of my way. / Know, Caesar dost not wrong, nor without cause / Will he be satisfied.

I must stop you, Cimber. This crouching and humble bowing might fire up the blood of ordinary men and turn what has already been decided into a child's game. Don't be so foolish as to think that Caesar's blood is so unruly that it can be melted from its true nature by what melts fools: I mean sweet words, low bows and the cringing of a spaniel. Your brother has been banished by law. If you bow and beg and fawn for him, I'll kick you out of my way like a dog. Know that Caesar does no wrong, and he will not be persuaded without good reason.
Is there no voice more worthy than my own, / To sound more sweetly in great Caesar's ear / For the repealing of my banish'd brother?
Is there no voice worthier than mine to sound sweeter in great Caesar's ear, to call back my banished brother?
I kiss thy hand, but not in flattery, Caesar; / Desiring thee that Publius Cimber may / Have an immediate freedom of repeal.
I kiss your hand, but not to flatter you, Caesar, asking you to let Publius Cimber be recalled at once.
Pardon, Caesar; Caesar, pardon: / As low as to thy foot doth Cassius fall, / To beg enfranchisement for Publius Cimber.
Pardon, Caesar! Caesar, pardon! Cassius falls as low as your foot to beg freedom for Publius Cimber.

I could be well mov'd, if I were as you; / If I could pray to move, prayers would move me: / But I am constant as the northern star, / Of whose true-fix'd and resting quality / There is no fellow in the firmament. / The skies are painted with unnumber'd sparks, / They are all fire, and every one doth shine; / But there's but one in all doth hold his place. / So in the world; 'tis furnish'd well with men, / And men are flesh and blood, and apprehensive; / Yet in the number I do know but one / That unassailable holds on his rank, / Unshak'd of motion: and that I am he, / Let me a little show it, even in this, / That I was constant Cimber should be banish'd, / And constant do remain to keep him so.

I could easily be moved if I were like you. If I could beg others to change their minds, other people's begging would move me. But I am as constant as the northern star, which has no equal in the sky for staying fixed and still. The skies are painted with countless sparks. They are all fire, and every one shines, but only one of them all keeps its place. It's the same on earth. It is well supplied with men, and men are flesh and blood and can think. Yet out of all of them I know only one who keeps his position without being shaken or moved, and that I am he, let me show a little, even in this: I was firm that Cimber should be banished, and I remain firm in keeping him banished.
Hence! wilt thou lift up Olympus?
Get away! Would you try to lift up Mount Olympus?
Even Brutus kneels in vain, doesn't he?
Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead! / Run hence, proclaim, cry it about the streets.
Liberty! Freedom! Tyranny is dead! Run from here, announce it, shout it through the streets.
Some to the common pulpits and cry out, / "Liberty, freedom, and enfranchisement!"
Some of you go to the public platforms and cry, "Liberty, freedom and release from slavery!"
People and Senators, be not affrighted. / Fly not; stand still; ambition's debt is paid.
People and senators, don't be frightened. Don't run; stand still. Ambition has paid its debt.
Go up to the platform, Brutus.
Here, quite confounded with this mutiny.
Here, completely stunned by this uprising.
Stand fast together, lest some friend of Caesar's / Should chance—
Stand firm together, in case some friend of Caesar's should happen—
Talk not of standing. Publius, good cheer! / There is no harm intended to your person, / Nor to no Roman else. So tell them, Publius.
Don't talk about standing firm. Publius, cheer up! No harm is meant to you or to any other Roman. Tell them so, Publius.
And leave us, Publius; lest that the people / Rushing on us, should do your age some mischief.
And leave us, Publius, in case the people rush at us and hurt you, an old man.
Do so; and let no man abide this deed / But we the doers.
Do that. And let no one answer for this deed except us who did it.
Fled to his house amaz'd. / Men, wives, and children stare, cry out, and run, / As it were doomsday.
He ran to his house in shock. Men, wives and children are staring, crying out and running, as if it were the end of the world.
Fates, we will know your pleasures. / That we shall die, we know; 'tis but the time / And drawing days out, that men stand upon.
Fates, we will soon know what you have in store for us. We know we will die; it's only the time, and how long they can spin their days out, that men care about.
Why, he that cuts off twenty years of life / Cuts off so many years of fearing death.
Why, whoever cuts off twenty years of a man's life cuts off that many years of fearing death.

Grant that, and then is death a benefit: / So are we Caesar's friends, that have abridg'd / His time of fearing death. Stoop, Romans, stoop, / And let us bathe our hands in Caesar's blood / Up to the elbows, and besmear our swords: / Then walk we forth, even to the market-place, / And waving our red weapons o'er our heads, / Let's all cry, "Peace, freedom, and liberty!"

Accept that, and then death is a favour. So we are Caesar's friends, who have shortened his time of fearing death. Bend down, Romans, bend down, and let us bathe our hands in Caesar's blood up to the elbows and smear our swords with it. Then let's walk out, right to the market-place, and, waving our red weapons over our heads, all shout, "Peace, freedom and liberty!"
Stoop then, and wash. How many ages hence / Shall this our lofty scene be acted over / In States unborn, and accents yet unknown!
Bend down, then, and wash. How many ages from now will this noble scene of ours be acted again, in countries not yet born and in languages not yet known!
How many times shall Caesar bleed in sport, / That now on Pompey's basis lies along, / No worthier than the dust!
How many times will Caesar bleed in plays, who now lies stretched out at the foot of Pompey's statue, worth no more than dust!
So oft as that shall be, / So often shall the knot of us be call'd / The men that gave their country liberty.
As often as that happens, our group will be called the men who gave their country liberty.
Ay, every man away. / Brutus shall lead; and we will grace his heels / With the most boldest and best hearts of Rome.
Yes, every man go. Brutus will lead, and we will follow at his heels in honour, the boldest and best hearts in Rome.
Soft, who comes here? A friend of Antony's.
Wait, who's this coming? A friend of Antony's.

Thus, Brutus, did my master bid me kneel; / Thus did Mark Antony bid me fall down; / And, being prostrate, thus he bade me say: / Brutus is noble, wise, valiant, and honest; / Caesar was mighty, bold, royal, and loving; / Say I love Brutus and I honour him; / Say I fear'd Caesar, honour'd him, and lov'd him. / If Brutus will vouchsafe that Antony / May safely come to him, and be resolv'd / How Caesar hath deserv'd to lie in death, / Mark Antony shall not love Caesar dead / So well as Brutus living; but will follow / The fortunes and affairs of noble Brutus / Thorough the hazards of this untrod state, / With all true faith. So says my master Antony.

Brutus, my master told me to kneel like this. Mark Antony told me to fall down like this, and when I lay at your feet, he told me to say this: Brutus is noble, wise, brave and honest; Caesar was mighty, bold, royal and loving. Say I love Brutus and honour him. Say I feared Caesar, honoured him and loved him. If Brutus will allow Antony to come to him safely and have it explained to him how Caesar deserved to die, Mark Antony will not love Caesar dead as much as Brutus living, but will follow noble Brutus's fortunes and affairs through all the dangers of this new state of things, with complete loyalty. That is what my master Antony says.
Thy master is a wise and valiant Roman; / I never thought him worse. / Tell him, so please him come unto this place, / He shall be satisfied and, by my honour, / Depart untouch'd.
Your master is a wise and brave Roman. I never thought him anything less. Tell him that if he cares to come here, his questions will be answered, and, on my honour, he will leave unharmed.
I know that we shall have him well to friend.
I know we will have him as a good friend.
I wish we may: but yet have I a mind / That fears him much; and my misgiving still / Falls shrewdly to the purpose.
I hope so. But I still have a feeling that fears him a lot, and my misgivings always turn out to be uncomfortably close to the mark.
But here comes Antony. Welcome, Mark Antony.
But here comes Antony. Welcome, Mark Antony.

O mighty Caesar! Dost thou lie so low? / Are all thy conquests, glories, triumphs, spoils, / Shrunk to this little measure? Fare thee well. / I know not, gentlemen, what you intend, / Who else must be let blood, who else is rank: / If I myself, there is no hour so fit / As Caesar's death's hour; nor no instrument / Of half that worth as those your swords, made rich / With the most noble blood of all this world. / I do beseech ye, if you bear me hard, / Now, whilst your purpled hands do reek and smoke, / Fulfill your pleasure. Live a thousand years, / I shall not find myself so apt to die. / No place will please me so, no means of death, / As here by Caesar, and by you cut off, / The choice and master spirits of this age.

Oh, mighty Caesar! Are you lying so low? Have all your conquests, glories, triumphs and spoils shrunk to this small space? Goodbye. I don't know, gentlemen, what you intend, who else must have blood let, who else is diseased. If it's me, there is no hour as fitting as the hour of Caesar's death, and no weapon half as worthy as your swords, made rich with the noblest blood in the whole world. I beg you, if you have something against me, do what you want now, while your bloodstained hands are still steaming. If I live a thousand years, I won't find myself so ready to die. No place will please me as much, and no way of dying, as here beside Caesar, cut down by you, the finest and most powerful spirits of this age.

O Antony, beg not your death of us. / Though now we must appear bloody and cruel, / As by our hands and this our present act / You see we do; yet see you but our hands / And this the bleeding business they have done. / Our hearts you see not; they are pitiful; / And pity to the general wrong of Rome— / As fire drives out fire, so pity pity— / Hath done this deed on Caesar. For your part, / To you our swords have leaden points, Mark Antony; / Our arms in strength of malice, and our hearts / Of brothers' temper, do receive you in / With all kind love, good thoughts, and reverence.

Oh, Antony, don't beg us for your death. Though we must look bloody and cruel now, as you can see from our hands and what we have just done, you only see our hands and the bleeding work they have done. You don't see our hearts. They are full of pity, and pity for the wrong done to all of Rome (as fire drives out fire, so pity drives out pity) has done this to Caesar. As for you, Mark Antony, our swords have blunt lead points. Our arms, though strong enough to seem hostile, and our hearts, full of brotherly feeling, welcome you in with all kind love, good thoughts and respect.
Your voice shall be as strong as any man's / In the disposing of new dignities.
Your voice will be as strong as anyone's in handing out the new offices of state.
Only be patient till we have appeas'd / The multitude, beside themselves with fear, / And then we will deliver you the cause / Why I, that did love Caesar when I struck him, / Have thus proceeded.
Only be patient until we have calmed the crowd, who are beside themselves with fear, and then we will explain to you why I, who loved Caesar even as I struck him, have acted as I have.

I doubt not of your wisdom. / Let each man render me his bloody hand. / First, Marcus Brutus, will I shake with you; / Next, Caius Cassius, do I take your hand. / Now, Decius Brutus, yours; now yours, Metellus; / Yours, Cinna; and, my valiant Casca, yours; / Though last, not least in love, yours, good Trebonius. / Gentlemen all—alas, what shall I say? / My credit now stands on such slippery ground, / That one of two bad ways you must conceit me, / Either a coward or a flatterer. / That I did love thee, Caesar, O, 'tis true: / If then thy spirit look upon us now, / Shall it not grieve thee dearer than thy death, / To see thy Antony making his peace, / Shaking the bloody fingers of thy foes, / Most noble, in the presence of thy corse? / Had I as many eyes as thou hast wounds, / Weeping as fast as they stream forth thy blood, / It would become me better than to close / In terms of friendship with thine enemies. / Pardon me, Julius! Here wast thou bay'd, brave hart; / Here didst thou fall; and here thy hunters stand, / Sign'd in thy spoil, and crimson'd in thy lethe. / O world, thou wast the forest to this hart; / And this indeed, O world, the heart of thee. / How like a deer strucken by many princes, / Dost thou here lie!

I don't doubt your wisdom. Let each man give me his bloody hand. First, Marcus Brutus, I'll shake yours. Next, Caius Cassius, I take your hand. Now, Decius Brutus, yours; now yours, Metellus; yours, Cinna; and, my brave Casca, yours. Last, but not least in my love, yours, good Trebonius. Gentlemen all—oh, what can I say? My reputation now stands on such slippery ground that you must think of me in one of two bad ways, either as a coward or as a flatterer. That I loved you, Caesar, oh, it's true! If your spirit is looking down on us now, won't it grieve you more than your death to see your Antony making his peace, shaking the bloody fingers of your enemies, most noble Caesar, in the presence of your body? If I had as many eyes as you have wounds, weeping as fast as they pour out your blood, it would suit me better than making friends with your enemies. Forgive me, Julius! Here you were cornered, brave stag. Here you fell, and here your hunters stand, marked with your slaughter and red with your lifeblood. Oh, world, you were the forest for this stag, and this, oh world, was truly your heart. How like a deer struck down by many princes you lie here!
Pardon me, Caius Cassius: / The enemies of Caesar shall say this; / Then, in a friend, it is cold modesty.
Forgive me, Caius Cassius. Even Caesar's enemies will say this, so from a friend it is only cool restraint.
I blame you not for praising Caesar so; / But what compact mean you to have with us? / Will you be prick'd in number of our friends, / Or shall we on, and not depend on you?
I don't blame you for praising Caesar like this. But what agreement do you mean to make with us? Will you be counted as one of our friends, or shall we go on without relying on you?

Therefore I took your hands; but was indeed / Sway'd from the point, by looking down on Caesar. / Friends am I with you all, and love you all, / Upon this hope, that you shall give me reasons / Why, and wherein, Caesar was dangerous.

That's why I took your hands, but I was distracted from the point by looking down at Caesar. I am friends with you all and love you all, in the hope that you will give me reasons why and in what way Caesar was dangerous.
Or else were this a savage spectacle. / Our reasons are so full of good regard / That were you, Antony, the son of Caesar, / You should be satisfied.
Otherwise this would be a savage sight. Our reasons are so well considered that even if you were Caesar's son, Antony, you would be satisfied.
That's all I seek, / And am moreover suitor that I may / Produce his body to the market-place; / And in the pulpit, as becomes a friend, / Speak in the order of his funeral.
That's all I ask. And I also ask that I may carry his body to the market-place and, in the pulpit, as a friend should, speak at his funeral.
Brutus, a word with you. / [Aside to Brutus] You know not what you do. Do not consent / That Antony speak in his funeral. / Know you how much the people may be mov'd / By that which he will utter?
Brutus, a word with you. [Aside to Brutus] You don't know what you're doing. Don't agree to let Antony speak at his funeral. Do you know how much the people may be stirred up by what he will say?

[Aside to Cassius] By your pardon: / I will myself into the pulpit first, / And show the reason of our Caesar's death. / What Antony shall speak, I will protest / He speaks by leave and by permission; / And that we are contented Caesar shall / Have all true rights and lawful ceremonies. / It shall advantage more than do us wrong.

[Aside to Cassius] Excuse me. I will go up into the pulpit first and explain the reason for Caesar's death. I'll announce that whatever Antony says, he says with our permission, and that we are happy for Caesar to have all the proper rites and lawful ceremonies. It will do us more good than harm.
[Aside to Brutus] I know not what may fall; I like it not.
[Aside to Brutus] I don't know what may happen. I don't like it.

Mark Antony, here, take you Caesar's body. / You shall not in your funeral speech blame us, / But speak all good you can devise of Caesar, / And say you do't by our permission; / Else shall you not have any hand at all / About his funeral. And you shall speak / In the same pulpit whereto I am going, / After my speech is ended.

Mark Antony, here, take Caesar's body. In your funeral speech you will not blame us, but say all the good you can think of about Caesar, and say you do it by our permission. Otherwise you won't have any part at all in his funeral. And you will speak in the same pulpit I am going to, after my speech is over.
Be it so; / I do desire no more.
So be it. I want nothing more.
Prepare the body, then, and follow us.
Prepare the body, then, and follow us.

O, pardon me, thou bleeding piece of earth, / That I am meek and gentle with these butchers. / Thou art the ruins of the noblest man / That ever lived in the tide of times. / Woe to the hand that shed this costly blood! / Over thy wounds now do I prophesy, / Which, like dumb mouths do ope their ruby lips / To beg the voice and utterance of my tongue, / A curse shall light upon the limbs of men; / Domestic fury and fierce civil strife / Shall cumber all the parts of Italy; / Blood and destruction shall be so in use, / And dreadful objects so familiar, / That mothers shall but smile when they behold / Their infants quartered with the hands of war; / All pity chok'd with custom of fell deeds: / And Caesar's spirit, ranging for revenge, / With Ate by his side come hot from Hell, / Shall in these confines with a monarch's voice / Cry havoc and let slip the dogs of war, / That this foul deed shall smell above the earth / With carrion men, groaning for burial.

Oh, forgive me, you bleeding piece of earth, for being meek and gentle with these butchers. You are the ruins of the noblest man who ever lived in the course of time. Woe to the hand that shed this precious blood! Over your wounds, which open their red lips like mouths that cannot speak, begging my tongue to speak for them, I now prophesy: a curse will fall on men's bodies. Fighting within families and fierce civil war will overrun every part of Italy. Blood and destruction will be so common, and dreadful sights so familiar, that mothers will only smile when they see their babies cut to pieces by the hands of war, all pity choked by the habit of cruel deeds. And Caesar's spirit, roaming for revenge, with Ate, goddess of ruin, hot from hell at his side, will cry "Havoc!" throughout this land in a king's voice and let loose the dogs of war, so that this foul deed will stink above the earth with rotting men groaning to be buried.
You serve Octavius Caesar, do you not?
You serve Octavius Caesar, don't you?
Caesar did write for him to come to Rome.
Caesar wrote for him to come to Rome.
He did receive his letters, and is coming, / And bid me say to you by word of mouth,— / [Seeing the body] O Caesar!
He received the letters and is on his way, and he told me to say to you in person— [Seeing the body] Oh, Caesar!
Thy heart is big, get thee apart and weep. / Passion, I see, is catching; for mine eyes, / Seeing those beads of sorrow stand in thine, / Began to water. Is thy master coming?
Your heart is full. Go aside and weep. Grief is catching, I see, because my eyes, seeing those drops of sorrow in yours, began to water. Is your master coming?
He lies tonight within seven leagues of Rome.
He is staying tonight within twenty miles of Rome.

Post back with speed, and tell him what hath chanc'd. / Here is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome, / No Rome of safety for Octavius yet. / Hie hence, and tell him so. Yet stay awhile; / Thou shalt not back till I have borne this corse / Into the market-place: there shall I try, / In my oration, how the people take / The cruel issue of these bloody men; / According to the which thou shalt discourse / To young Octavius of the state of things. / Lend me your hand.

Ride back fast and tell him what has happened. This is a mourning Rome, a dangerous Rome, not yet a safe Rome for Octavius. Hurry and tell him so. But wait a moment. Don't go back until I have carried this body into the market-place. There, in my speech, I will test how the people take the cruel act of these bloody men, and according to that you will report to young Octavius how things stand. Give me a hand.
We will be satisfied; let us be satisfied.
We want an explanation. Give us an explanation.

Then follow me, and give me audience, friends. / Cassius, go you into the other street / And part the numbers. / Those that will hear me speak, let 'em stay here; / Those that will follow Cassius, go with him; / And public reasons shall be rendered / Of Caesar's death.

Then follow me and listen to me, friends. Cassius, you go into the other street and divide the crowd. Those who want to hear me speak, stay here. Those who want to follow Cassius, go with him. And the reasons for Caesar's death will be given publicly.
I will hear Cassius; and compare their reasons, / When severally we hear them rendered.
I'll hear Cassius, and we can compare their reasons when we've heard them separately.
The noble Brutus is ascended: silence!
Noble Brutus has gone up. Quiet!

Be patient till the last. / Romans, countrymen, and lovers, hear me for my cause; and be silent, / that you may hear. Believe me for mine honour, and have respect to mine / honour, that you may believe. Censure me in your wisdom, and awake your / senses, that you may the better judge. If there be any in this / assembly, any dear friend of Caesar's, to him I say that Brutus' love / to Caesar was no less than his. If then that friend demand why Brutus / rose against Caesar, this is my answer: Not that I loved Caesar less, / but that I loved Rome more. Had you rather Caesar were living, and die / all slaves, than that Caesar were dead, to live all free men? As Caesar / loved me, I weep for him; as he was fortunate, I rejoice at it; as he / was valiant, I honour him; but, as he was ambitious, I slew him. There / is tears, for his love; joy for his fortune; honour for his valour; and / death, for his ambition. Who is here so base, that would be a bondman? / If any, speak; for him have I offended. Who is here so rude, that would / not be a Roman? If any, speak; for him have I offended. Who is here so / vile, that will not love his country? If any, speak; for him have I / offended. I pause for a reply.

Be patient until I've finished. Romans, countrymen and friends, hear me for the sake of my cause, and be silent so that you can hear. Believe me because of my honour, and respect my honour so that you can believe me. Judge me with your wisdom, and wake up your minds so that you can judge better. If there is anyone in this crowd, any dear friend of Caesar's, I say to him that Brutus's love for Caesar was no less than his. If that friend then asks why Brutus rose against Caesar, this is my answer: not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more. Would you rather Caesar were alive and all of you died slaves, than that Caesar were dead and all of you lived as free men? Because Caesar loved me, I weep for him; because he was fortunate, I rejoice at it; because he was brave, I honour him; but because he was ambitious, I killed him. There are tears for his love, joy for his good fortune, honour for his courage and death for his ambition. Who here is so low that he would be a slave? If anyone, speak, because I have offended him. Who here is so uncivilised that he would not be a Roman? If anyone, speak, because I have offended him. Who here is so vile that he will not love his country? If anyone, speak, because I have offended him. I pause for a reply.

Then none have I offended. I have done no more to Caesar than you shall / do to Brutus. The question of his death is enroll'd in the Capitol, his / glory not extenuated, wherein he was worthy; nor his offences enforc'd, / for which he suffered death.

Then I have offended no one. I have done no more to Caesar than you would do to Brutus. The reasons for his death are recorded in the Capitol. His glory has not been played down where he deserved it, nor his offences exaggerated, for which he suffered death.

Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony, who, though he had no hand / in his death, shall receive the benefit of his dying, a place in the / commonwealth; as which of you shall not? With this I depart, that, as I / slew my best lover for the good of Rome, I have the same dagger for / myself, when it shall please my country to need my death.

Here comes his body, mourned by Mark Antony, who, though he had no part in his death, will receive the benefit of his dying, a place in the free state, as will every one of you. With this I leave you: as I killed my best friend for the good of Rome, I have the same dagger for myself whenever my country needs my death.
Bring him with triumph home unto his house.
Carry him home to his house in triumph.
Give him a statue with his ancestors.
Give him a statue alongside his ancestors.
Caesar's better parts / Shall be crown'd in Brutus.
The best parts of Caesar will be crowned in Brutus.
We'll bring him to his house with shouts and clamours.
We'll take him to his house with shouting and cheering.

Good countrymen, let me depart alone, / And, for my sake, stay here with Antony. / Do grace to Caesar's corpse, and grace his speech / Tending to Caesar's glories, which Mark Antony, / By our permission, is allow'd to make. / I do entreat you, not a man depart, / Save I alone, till Antony have spoke.

Good countrymen, let me go alone, and, for my sake, stay here with Antony. Honour Caesar's body, and honour his speech about Caesar's glories, which Mark Antony is allowed to make by our permission. I beg you, let no one leave except me until Antony has spoken.
Stay, ho! and let us hear Mark Antony.
Let him go up into the public chair. / We'll hear him. Noble Antony, go up.
Let him go up to the public platform. We'll hear him. Noble Antony, go up.
For Brutus' sake, I am beholding to you.
For Brutus's sake, I am grateful to you.
What does he say of Brutus?
He says, for Brutus' sake / He finds himself beholding to us all.
He says that for Brutus's sake he is grateful to all of us.
'Twere best he speak no harm of Brutus here!
He'd better not say anything bad about Brutus here!
Nay, that's certain. / We are blest that Rome is rid of him.
Yes, that's certain. We are lucky Rome is rid of him.
Peace! let us hear what Antony can say.
Quiet! Let's hear what Antony has to say.
Peace, ho! let us hear him.

Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears; / I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him. / The evil that men do lives after them, / The good is oft interred with their bones; / So let it be with Caesar. The noble Brutus / Hath told you Caesar was ambitious. / If it were so, it was a grievous fault, / And grievously hath Caesar answer'd it. / Here, under leave of Brutus and the rest, / For Brutus is an honourable man, / So are they all, all honourable men, / Come I to speak in Caesar's funeral. / He was my friend, faithful and just to me; / But Brutus says he was ambitious, / And Brutus is an honourable man. / He hath brought many captives home to Rome, / Whose ransoms did the general coffers fill: / Did this in Caesar seem ambitious? / When that the poor have cried, Caesar hath wept; / Ambition should be made of sterner stuff: / Yet Brutus says he was ambitious; / And Brutus is an honourable man. / You all did see that on the Lupercal / I thrice presented him a kingly crown, / Which he did thrice refuse. Was this ambition? / Yet Brutus says he was ambitious; / And sure he is an honourable man. / I speak not to disprove what Brutus spoke, / But here I am to speak what I do know. / You all did love him once, not without cause; / What cause withholds you then to mourn for him? / O judgement, thou art fled to brutish beasts, / And men have lost their reason. Bear with me. / My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar, / And I must pause till it come back to me.

Friends, Romans, countrymen, listen to me. I have come to bury Caesar, not to praise him. The evil that men do lives on after them; the good is often buried with their bones. Let it be so with Caesar. The noble Brutus has told you that Caesar was ambitious. If that was so, it was a serious fault, and Caesar has paid seriously for it. Here, with the permission of Brutus and the rest (for Brutus is an honourable man; so are they all, all honourable men), I have come to speak at Caesar's funeral. He was my friend, faithful and fair to me. But Brutus says he was ambitious, and Brutus is an honourable man. He brought many captives home to Rome, whose ransoms filled the public treasury. Did this seem ambitious in Caesar? When the poor cried, Caesar wept. Ambition should be made of harder stuff. Yet Brutus says he was ambitious, and Brutus is an honourable man. You all saw that at the Lupercal I offered him a king's crown three times, and three times he refused it. Was this ambition? Yet Brutus says he was ambitious, and he is certainly an honourable man. I'm not speaking to disprove what Brutus said, but I am here to say what I know. You all loved him once, and not without reason. What reason stops you mourning for him, then? Oh, judgement, you have run away to the brute beasts, and men have lost their reason. Bear with me. My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar, and I must pause until it comes back to me.
Methinks there is much reason in his sayings.
I think there's a lot of sense in what he says.
If thou consider rightly of the matter, / Caesar has had great wrong.
If you think about it properly, Caesar has been greatly wronged.
Has he, masters? / I fear there will a worse come in his place.
Has he, friends? I'm afraid someone worse will come in his place.
Mark'd ye his words? He would not take the crown; / Therefore 'tis certain he was not ambitious.
Did you notice what he said? He wouldn't take the crown. So it's certain he wasn't ambitious.
If it be found so, some will dear abide it.
If that turns out to be true, someone will pay dearly for it.
Poor soul, his eyes are red as fire with weeping.
Poor man, his eyes are red as fire from weeping.
There's not a nobler man in Rome than Antony.
There isn't a nobler man in Rome than Antony.
Now mark him; he begins again to speak.
Now listen to him. He's starting to speak again.

But yesterday the word of Caesar might / Have stood against the world; now lies he there, / And none so poor to do him reverence. / O masters! If I were dispos'd to stir / Your hearts and minds to mutiny and rage, / I should do Brutus wrong and Cassius wrong, / Who, you all know, are honourable men. / I will not do them wrong; I rather choose / To wrong the dead, to wrong myself and you, / Than I will wrong such honourable men. / But here's a parchment with the seal of Caesar, / I found it in his closet; 'tis his will: / Let but the commons hear this testament, / Which, pardon me, I do not mean to read, / And they would go and kiss dead Caesar's wounds, / And dip their napkins in his sacred blood; / Yea, beg a hair of him for memory, / And, dying, mention it within their wills, / Bequeathing it as a rich legacy / Unto their issue.

Only yesterday the word of Caesar could have stood against the whole world. Now he lies there, and no one is so low as to show him respect. Oh, friends! If I wanted to stir your hearts and minds to rebellion and rage, I would wrong Brutus and wrong Cassius, who, you all know, are honourable men. I will not wrong them. I would rather wrong the dead, wrong myself and you, than wrong such honourable men. But here's a document with Caesar's seal. I found it in his study. It's his will. If the common people could only hear this will (which, forgive me, I don't intend to read), they would go and kiss dead Caesar's wounds and dip their handkerchiefs in his sacred blood, yes, beg for a hair of his to remember him by, and when they died they would mention it in their own wills, leaving it as a precious inheritance to their children.
We'll hear the will. Read it, Mark Antony.
We'll hear the will. Read it, Mark Antony.
The will, the will! We will hear Caesar's will.
The will, the will! We want to hear Caesar's will.

Have patience, gentle friends, I must not read it. / It is not meet you know how Caesar loved you. / You are not wood, you are not stones, but men; / And being men, hearing the will of Caesar, / It will inflame you, it will make you mad. / 'Tis good you know not that you are his heirs; / For if you should, O, what would come of it?

Be patient, gentle friends. I mustn't read it. It isn't right for you to know how much Caesar loved you. You are not wood, you are not stones, but men, and being men, hearing Caesar's will would inflame you, it would drive you mad. It's better you don't know you are his heirs, because if you did, oh, what would come of it?
Read the will! We'll hear it, Antony; / You shall read us the will, Caesar's will!
Read the will! We'll hear it, Antony. You must read us the will, Caesar's will!
Will you be patient? Will you stay awhile? / I have o'ershot myself to tell you of it. / I fear I wrong the honourable men / Whose daggers have stabb'd Caesar; I do fear it.
Will you be patient? Will you wait a little? I have gone too far in telling you about it. I'm afraid I'm wronging the honourable men whose daggers stabbed Caesar. I really am afraid of it.
They were villains, murderers. The will! Read the will!
They were villains, murderers. The will! Read the will!
You will compel me then to read the will? / Then make a ring about the corpse of Caesar, / And let me show you him that made the will. / Shall I descend? and will you give me leave?
So you will force me to read the will? Then make a ring around Caesar's body, and let me show you the man who made the will. Shall I come down? Will you allow me?
Stand from the hearse, stand from the body.
Stand back from the coffin, stand back from the body.
Room for Antony, most noble Antony!
Make room for Antony, most noble Antony!
Nay, press not so upon me; stand far off.
No, don't crowd me like that. Stand further off.
Stand back! Make room! Get back.

If you have tears, prepare to shed them now. / You all do know this mantle. I remember / The first time ever Caesar put it on; / 'Twas on a Summer's evening, in his tent, / That day he overcame the Nervii. / Look, in this place ran Cassius' dagger through: / See what a rent the envious Casca made: / Through this the well-beloved Brutus stabb'd; / And as he pluck'd his cursed steel away, / Mark how the blood of Caesar follow'd it, / As rushing out of doors, to be resolv'd / If Brutus so unkindly knock'd, or no; / For Brutus, as you know, was Caesar's angel. / Judge, O you gods, how dearly Caesar lov'd him. / This was the most unkindest cut of all; / For when the noble Caesar saw him stab, / Ingratitude, more strong than traitors' arms, / Quite vanquish'd him: then burst his mighty heart; / And in his mantle muffling up his face, / Even at the base of Pompey's statue / Which all the while ran blood, great Caesar fell. / O, what a fall was there, my countrymen! / Then I, and you, and all of us fell down, / Whilst bloody treason flourish'd over us. / O, now you weep; and I perceive you feel / The dint of pity. These are gracious drops. / Kind souls, what weep you when you but behold / Our Caesar's vesture wounded? Look you here, / Here is himself, marr'd, as you see, with traitors.

If you have tears, get ready to shed them now. You all know this cloak. I remember the first time Caesar ever put it on. It was a summer evening in his tent, the day he defeated the Nervii. Look, here is where Cassius's dagger went through. See what a tear spiteful Casca made. Through this one the much-loved Brutus stabbed, and as he pulled his cursed steel away, see how Caesar's blood followed it, as if rushing out of doors to find out for certain whether it really was Brutus knocking so unkindly or not. Because Brutus, as you know, was Caesar's darling. Judge, you gods, how dearly Caesar loved him! This was the most unkind cut of all. Because when noble Caesar saw him stab, ingratitude, stronger than traitors' weapons, completely defeated him. Then his mighty heart burst, and, covering his face with his cloak, great Caesar fell at the foot of Pompey's statue, which ran with blood all the while. Oh, what a fall that was, my countrymen! Then I and you and all of us fell down, while bloody treason triumphed over us. Oh, now you are weeping, and I see you feel the force of pity. These are gracious tears. Kind souls, why do you weep when you only see our Caesar's clothes wounded? Look here, here is the man himself, mutilated, as you see, by traitors.
Revenge! Go! Search! Burn! Fire! Kill! Slay! Don't let a traitor live!
Peace there! Hear the noble Antony.
Quiet there! Listen to noble Antony.
We'll hear him, we'll follow him, we'll die with him.
We'll listen to him, we'll follow him, we'll die with him.

Good friends, sweet friends, let me not stir you up / To such a sudden flood of mutiny. / They that have done this deed are honourable. / What private griefs they have, alas, I know not, / That made them do it. They're wise and honourable, / And will, no doubt, with reasons answer you. / I come not, friends, to steal away your hearts. / I am no orator, as Brutus is; / But, as you know me all, a plain blunt man, / That love my friend; and that they know full well / That gave me public leave to speak of him. / For I have neither wit, nor words, nor worth, / Action, nor utterance, nor the power of speech, / To stir men's blood. I only speak right on. / I tell you that which you yourselves do know, / Show you sweet Caesar's wounds, poor poor dumb mouths, / And bid them speak for me. But were I Brutus, / And Brutus Antony, there were an Antony / Would ruffle up your spirits, and put a tongue / In every wound of Caesar, that should move / The stones of Rome to rise and mutiny.

Good friends, sweet friends, don't let me stir you up into such a sudden flood of rebellion. The men who did this deed are honourable. What private grudges they had that made them do it, alas, I don't know. They are wise and honourable, and no doubt they will give you reasons. I haven't come, friends, to steal your hearts. I am no speaker, as Brutus is, but, as you all know, a plain, blunt man who loves his friend, and the men who gave me public permission to speak about him know that very well. Because I have neither cleverness, nor words, nor standing, nor gestures, nor delivery, nor the power of speech to stir men's blood. I just speak straight out. I tell you what you already know, show you sweet Caesar's wounds, poor, poor speechless mouths, and tell them to speak for me. But if I were Brutus, and Brutus were Antony, then there would be an Antony who would stir up your spirits and put a tongue in every one of Caesar's wounds that would move the very stones of Rome to rise up and rebel.
We'll burn the house of Brutus.
Away, then! come, seek the conspirators.
Let's go, then! Come on, find the conspirators.
Yet hear me, countrymen; yet hear me speak.
Still, listen to me, countrymen. Still, hear me speak.
Peace, ho! Hear Antony; most noble Antony.
Quiet! Listen to Antony, most noble Antony.
Why, friends, you go to do you know not what. / Wherein hath Caesar thus deserved your loves? / Alas, you know not; I must tell you then. / You have forgot the will I told you of.
Why, friends, you're going off to do you don't know what. How has Caesar earned your love like this? Oh, you don't know. Then I must tell you. You have forgotten the will I told you about.
Most true; the will!—let's stay, and hear the will.
Very true. The will! Let's stay and hear the will.
Here is the will, and under Caesar's seal. / To every Roman citizen he gives, / To every several man, seventy-five drachmas.
Here is the will, under Caesar's seal. To every Roman citizen, to every single man, he gives seventy-five drachmas.
Most noble Caesar! We'll revenge his death.
Most noble Caesar! We'll avenge his death.

Moreover, he hath left you all his walks, / His private arbors, and new-planted orchards, / On this side Tiber; he hath left them you, / And to your heirs forever; common pleasures, / To walk abroad, and recreate yourselves. / Here was a Caesar! when comes such another?

What's more, he has left you all his walks, his private gardens and his newly planted orchards on this side of the Tiber. He has left them to you and your heirs for ever, as public parks to walk in and enjoy yourselves. That was a Caesar! When will there be another like him?
Never, never. Come, away, away! / We'll burn his body in the holy place, / And with the brands fire the traitors' houses. / Take up the body.
Never, never! Come on, away, away! We'll burn his body in the holy place and use the burning wood to set fire to the traitors' houses. Pick up the body.
Now let it work. Mischief, thou art afoot, / Take thou what course thou wilt!
Now let it work. Trouble, you are on the move. Take whatever course you like!
Sir, Octavius is already come to Rome.
Sir, Octavius has already arrived in Rome.
He and Lepidus are at Caesar's house.
He and Lepidus are at Caesar's house.
And thither will I straight to visit him. / He comes upon a wish. Fortune is merry, / And in this mood will give us anything.
And I'll go straight there to see him. He comes just when I wanted him. Fortune is in a good mood, and while she's like this she'll give us anything.
I heard him say Brutus and Cassius / Are rid like madmen through the gates of Rome.
I heard him say that Brutus and Cassius have ridden like madmen out through the gates of Rome.
Belike they had some notice of the people, / How I had moved them. Bring me to Octavius.
Perhaps they heard how I had stirred up the people. Take me to Octavius.
I dreamt tonight that I did feast with Caesar, / And things unluckily charge my fantasy. / I have no will to wander forth of doors, / Yet something leads me forth.
Last night I dreamt I was feasting with Caesar, and things weigh on my imagination like a bad omen. I have no wish to go out of doors, and yet something leads me out.
Are you a married man or a bachelor?
Are you a married man or a bachelor?
Ay, and truly, you were best.
Yes, and truthfully, if you know what's good for you.
What is my name? Whither am I going? Where do I dwell? Am I a married / man or a bachelor? Then, to answer every man directly and briefly, / wisely and truly. Wisely I say I am a bachelor.
What's my name? Where am I going? Where do I live? Am I a married man or a bachelor? Then, to answer every man straight and briefly, wisely and truthfully: wisely, I say I'm a bachelor.
That's as much as to say they are fools that marry; you'll bear me a / bang for that, I fear. Proceed, directly.
That's as good as saying people who marry are fools. You'll get a punch from me for that, I'm afraid. Go on, straight.
Directly, I am going to Caesar's funeral.
Straight, I'm going to Caesar's funeral.
As a friend, or an enemy?
As a friend or an enemy?
Briefly, I dwell by the Capitol.
Briefly, I live near the Capitol.
Tear him to pieces! He's a conspirator.
Tear him to pieces! He's a conspirator.
I am Cinna the poet, I am Cinna the poet.
I'm Cinna the poet, I'm Cinna the poet.
Tear him for his bad verses, tear him for his bad verses.
Tear him for his bad poems, tear him for his bad poems.
I am not Cinna the conspirator.
It is no matter, his name's Cinna; pluck but his name out of his heart, / and turn him going.
It doesn't matter. His name's Cinna. Just tear his name out of his heart and send him on his way.
Tear him, tear him! Come; brands, ho! firebrands. To Brutus', to / Cassius'; burn all. Some to Decius' house, and some to Casca's, some to / Ligarius'. Away, go!
Tear him, tear him! Come on, torches! Burning torches! To Brutus's, to Cassius's, burn them all. Some to Decius's house, some to Casca's, some to Ligarius's. Away, go!
These many then shall die; their names are prick'd.
So these men will die. Their names are marked.
Your brother too must die; consent you, Lepidus?
Your brother must die too. Do you agree, Lepidus?
Upon condition Publius shall not live, / Who is your sister's son, Mark Antony.
On condition that Publius doesn't live either, who is your sister's son, Mark Antony.
He shall not live; look, with a spot I damn him. / But, Lepidus, go you to Caesar's house; / Fetch the will hither, and we shall determine / How to cut off some charge in legacies.
He won't live. Look, with a mark I condemn him. But, Lepidus, go to Caesar's house and bring the will here, and we'll work out how to cut some of the costs of his bequests.
What, shall I find you here?
What, will I find you here?
Or here, or at the Capitol.
Either here or at the Capitol.
This is a slight unmeritable man, / Meet to be sent on errands. Is it fit, / The three-fold world divided, he should stand / One of the three to share it?
He is an insignificant, worthless man, fit to be sent on errands. Is it right, when the world is divided into three, that he should be one of the three to share it?
So you thought him, / And took his voice who should be prick'd to die / In our black sentence and proscription.
That's what you thought of him, and you took his opinion on who should be marked down to die in our black list of death sentences.

Octavius, I have seen more days than you; / And though we lay these honours on this man, / To ease ourselves of divers sland'rous loads, / He shall but bear them as the ass bears gold, / To groan and sweat under the business, / Either led or driven, as we point the way; / And having brought our treasure where we will, / Then take we down his load, and turn him off, / Like to the empty ass, to shake his ears, / And graze in commons.

Octavius, I have lived longer than you. And though we give these honours to this man to take some of the blame off ourselves, he will only carry them as a donkey carries gold, groaning and sweating under the work, either led or driven, as we point the way. And when he has carried our treasure where we want it, then we take off his load and turn him out, like an unloaded donkey, to shake his ears and graze on the common.
You may do your will; / But he's a tried and valiant soldier.
You can do what you like, but he's an experienced and brave soldier.

So is my horse, Octavius; and for that / I do appoint him store of provender. / It is a creature that I teach to fight, / To wind, to stop, to run directly on, / His corporal motion govern'd by my spirit. / And, in some taste, is Lepidus but so: / He must be taught, and train'd, and bid go forth: / A barren-spirited fellow; one that feeds / On objects, arts, and imitations, / Which, out of use and stal'd by other men, / Begin his fashion. Do not talk of him / But as a property. And now, Octavius, / Listen great things. Brutus and Cassius / Are levying powers; we must straight make head. / Therefore let our alliance be combin'd, / Our best friends made, our means stretch'd; / And let us presently go sit in council, / How covert matters may be best disclos'd, / And open perils surest answered.

So is my horse, Octavius, and for that I give him a supply of food. It is a creature I teach to fight, to turn, to stop, to run straight on, its bodily movements controlled by my mind. And in some ways Lepidus is just like that. He has to be taught and trained and told to go. He's a man with no ideas of his own, who lives on curiosities, skills and fashions that have already been used up and grown stale with other men before he takes them up. Don't talk of him except as a tool. And now, Octavius, listen to important things. Brutus and Cassius are raising armies. We must raise a force at once. So let's join our alliance together, gather our best friends and stretch our resources as far as they will go, and let's sit down in council at once to decide how hidden dangers can best be discovered and open dangers most safely met.
Let us do so: for we are at the stake, / And bay'd about with many enemies; / And some that smile have in their hearts, I fear, / Millions of mischiefs.
Let's do that, because we are like a bear tied to the stake, surrounded by many enemies barking at us. And some who smile have millions of evil plans in their hearts, I fear.
Give the word, ho! and stand.
What now, Lucilius! is Cassius near?
What news, Lucilius? Is Cassius near?
He is at hand, and Pindarus is come / To do you salutation from his master.
He's close by, and Pindarus has come to greet you from his master.
He greets me well. Your master, Pindarus, / In his own change, or by ill officers, / Hath given me some worthy cause to wish / Things done, undone: but, if he be at hand, / I shall be satisfied.

He sends his greetings by a good man. Your master, Pindarus, either through his own change of heart or through bad officers, has given me good reason to wish some things undone that have been done. But if he's nearby, I'll get an explanation.
I do not doubt / But that my noble master will appear / Such as he is, full of regard and honour.
I'm sure my noble master will show himself as he is, worthy of respect and honour.
He is not doubted. A word, Lucilius; / How he received you, let me be resolv'd.
I don't doubt him. A word, Lucilius. Tell me how he received you.
With courtesy and with respect enough, / But not with such familiar instances, / Nor with such free and friendly conference, / As he hath us'd of old.
With courtesy and with enough respect, but not with the friendly gestures or such free and open talk as he used to.

Thou hast describ'd / A hot friend cooling. Ever note, Lucilius, / When love begins to sicken and decay / It useth an enforced ceremony. / There are no tricks in plain and simple faith; / But hollow men, like horses hot at hand, / Make gallant show and promise of their mettle;

You have described a warm friend cooling. Always notice, Lucilius, that when love begins to sicken and decay, it uses forced politeness. There are no tricks in plain and simple loyalty. But hollow men, like horses that are lively when held, make a fine show and promise of their spirit,
But when they should endure the bloody spur, / They fall their crests, and like deceitful jades / Sink in the trial. Comes his army on?
but when they should endure the bloody spur, they drop their heads and, like worthless old nags, fail when tested. Is his army coming?
They meant this night in Sardis to be quarter'd; / The greater part, the horse in general, / Are come with Cassius.
They meant to camp tonight in Sardis. Most of them, all the cavalry, have come with Cassius.
Hark! he is arriv'd. / March gently on to meet him.
Listen! He has arrived. March slowly forward to meet him.
Stand, ho! Speak the word along.
Most noble brother, you have done me wrong.
Most noble brother, you have wronged me.
Judge me, you gods; wrong I mine enemies? / And if not so, how should I wrong a brother?
Judge me, you gods! Do I wrong even my enemies? And if not, how would I wrong a brother?
Brutus, this sober form of yours hides wrongs; / And when you do them—
Brutus, this serious manner of yours hides wrongs, and when you do them—

Cassius, be content. / Speak your griefs softly, I do know you well. / Before the eyes of both our armies here, / Which should perceive nothing but love from us, / Let us not wrangle. Bid them move away; / Then in my tent, Cassius, enlarge your griefs, / And I will give you audience.

Cassius, calm down. Speak your complaints quietly. I know you well. In front of both our armies here, who should see nothing but love from us, let's not quarrel. Tell them to move away. Then in my tent, Cassius, set out your complaints in full, and I will listen.
Pindarus, / Bid our commanders lead their charges off / A little from this ground.
Pindarus, tell our commanders to lead their troops a little way off from here.
Lucilius, do you the like; and let no man / Come to our tent till we have done our conference. / Lucius and Titinius, guard our door.
Lucilius, you do the same, and let no one come to our tent until we've finished our talk. Lucius and Titinius, guard our door.

That you have wrong'd me doth appear in this: / You have condemn'd and noted Lucius Pella / For taking bribes here of the Sardians; / Wherein my letters, praying on his side / Because I knew the man, were slighted off.

That you have wronged me is clear from this: you have condemned and disgraced Lucius Pella for taking bribes here from the people of Sardis, and my letters pleading for him, because I knew the man, were brushed aside.
You wrong'd yourself to write in such a case.
You wronged yourself by writing in such a case.
In such a time as this it is not meet / That every nice offence should bear his comment.
At a time like this it isn't right that every petty offence should be criticised.
Let me tell you, Cassius, you yourself / Are much condemn'd to have an itching palm, / To sell and mart your offices for gold / To undeservers.
Let me tell you, Cassius, that you yourself are much blamed for having an itching palm, for selling and trading your offices for gold to people who don't deserve them.
I an itching palm! / You know that you are Brutus that speak this, / Or, by the gods, this speech were else your last.
I have an itching palm! You know that you are Brutus, saying this, or, by the gods, this speech would be your last.
The name of Cassius honours this corruption, / And chastisement doth therefore hide his head.
The name of Cassius makes this corruption look respectable, so punishment hides its head.

Remember March, the Ides of March remember: / Did not great Julius bleed for justice' sake? / What villain touch'd his body, that did stab, / And not for justice? What! Shall one of us, / That struck the foremost man of all this world / But for supporting robbers, shall we now / Contaminate our fingers with base bribes, / And sell the mighty space of our large honours / For so much trash as may be grasped thus? / I had rather be a dog, and bay the moon, / Than such a Roman.

Remember March, remember the fifteenth of March. Didn't great Julius bleed for the sake of justice? What villain touched his body and stabbed him, except for justice? What, shall one of us who struck down the greatest man in all this world just for protecting robbers, shall we now dirty our fingers with low bribes and sell the great range of our high honours for as much trash as can be grabbed like this? I would rather be a dog and howl at the moon than be a Roman like that.
Brutus, bait not me, / I'll not endure it. You forget yourself, / To hedge me in. I am a soldier, I, / Older in practice, abler than yourself / To make conditions.
Brutus, don't bait me. I won't stand for it. You forget yourself when you try to restrict me. I am a soldier, I am, more experienced and better able than you to manage affairs.
Go to; you are not, Cassius.
Urge me no more, I shall forget myself; / Have mind upon your health, tempt me no farther.
Don't push me any further, or I'll forget myself. Think of your safety. Don't provoke me any more.
Hear me, for I will speak. / Must I give way and room to your rash choler? / Shall I be frighted when a madman stares?
Listen to me, because I will speak. Must I give way to your hot temper? Shall I be frightened when a madman stares at me?
O ye gods, ye gods! Must I endure all this?
Oh, you gods, you gods! Must I put up with all this?

All this? ay, more: fret till your proud heart break; / Go show your slaves how choleric you are, / And make your bondmen tremble. Must I budge? / Must I observe you? Must I stand and crouch / Under your testy humour? By the gods, / You shall digest the venom of your spleen, / Though it do split you; for, from this day forth, / I'll use you for my mirth, yea, for my laughter, / When you are waspish.

All this? Yes, more. Fume until your proud heart breaks. Go and show your slaves how bad-tempered you are, and make your servants tremble. Must I flinch? Must I treat you with respect? Must I stand and cower under your irritable mood? By the gods, you will swallow the poison of your own anger, even if it splits you open, because from today on I'll use you for my amusement, yes, for my laughter, when you are being waspish.
You say you are a better soldier: / Let it appear so; make your vaunting true, / And it shall please me well. For mine own part, / I shall be glad to learn of noble men.
You say you are a better soldier. Let it be seen. Prove your boasting true, and I'll be very pleased. For my part, I'll be glad to learn from noble men.
You wrong me every way, you wrong me, Brutus. / I said, an elder soldier, not a better: / Did I say better?
You wrong me in every way. You wrong me, Brutus. I said an older soldier, not a better one. Did I say better?
If you did, I care not.
If you did, I don't care.
When Caesar liv'd, he durst not thus have mov'd me.
When Caesar was alive, he wouldn't have dared to provoke me like this.
Peace, peace! you durst not so have tempted him.
Quiet, quiet! You wouldn't have dared to provoke him like this.
What? Wouldn't have dared to provoke him?
For your life you durst not.
Do not presume too much upon my love. / I may do that I shall be sorry for.
Don't count too much on my love. I may do something I'll be sorry for.

You have done that you should be sorry for. / There is no terror, Cassius, in your threats, / For I am arm'd so strong in honesty, / That they pass by me as the idle wind, / Which I respect not. I did send to you / For certain sums of gold, which you denied me; / For I can raise no money by vile means: / By Heaven, I had rather coin my heart, / And drop my blood for drachmas, than to wring / From the hard hands of peasants their vile trash / By any indirection. I did send / To you for gold to pay my legions, / Which you denied me: was that done like Cassius? / Should I have answer'd Caius Cassius so? / When Marcus Brutus grows so covetous, / To lock such rascal counters from his friends, / Be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts, / Dash him to pieces!

You have done something you should be sorry for. There is nothing frightening in your threats, Cassius, because I am so strongly armed with honesty that they pass me by like the empty wind, which I ignore. I sent to you for certain sums of gold, which you refused me, because I can't raise money by dishonest means. By heaven, I would rather mint my heart into coins and drop my blood for drachmas than squeeze their wretched pennies out of the hard hands of peasants by crooked means. I sent to you for gold to pay my legions, which you refused me. Was that done like Cassius? Would I have answered Caius Cassius like that? When Marcus Brutus grows so greedy that he locks such worthless coins away from his friends, be ready, gods, with all your thunderbolts, and smash him to pieces!
I did not. He was but a fool / That brought my answer back. Brutus hath riv'd my heart. / A friend should bear his friend's infirmities; / But Brutus makes mine greater than they are.
I did not. The man who brought back my answer was a fool. Brutus has split my heart. A friend should put up with his friend's weaknesses, but Brutus makes mine bigger than they are.
I do not, till you practise them on me.
I don't, until you use them against me.
I do not like your faults.
A friendly eye could never see such faults.
A friendly eye could never see such faults.
A flatterer's would not, though they do appear / As huge as high Olympus.
A flatterer's eye wouldn't, even if they looked as huge as high Mount Olympus.

Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come, / Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius, / For Cassius is a-weary of the world: / Hated by one he loves; brav'd by his brother; / Check'd like a bondman; all his faults observ'd, / Set in a note-book, learn'd and conn'd by rote, / To cast into my teeth. O, I could weep / My spirit from mine eyes! There is my dagger, / And here my naked breast; within, a heart / Dearer than Plutus' mine, richer than gold: / If that thou be'st a Roman, take it forth. / I, that denied thee gold, will give my heart: / Strike as thou didst at Caesar; for I know, / When thou didst hate him worst, thou lovedst him better / Than ever thou lovedst Cassius.

Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come, take your revenge on Cassius alone, because Cassius is tired of the world: hated by someone he loves, defied by his brother, scolded like a slave, all his faults watched, written in a notebook, studied and learned by heart to throw in my face. Oh, I could weep my spirit out through my eyes! There is my dagger, and here is my bare chest, and inside it a heart more precious than the mines of Plutus, god of riches, richer than gold. If you are a Roman, take it out. I, who refused you gold, will give you my heart. Strike as you did at Caesar, because I know that when you hated him most, you loved him more than you ever loved Cassius.

Sheathe your dagger. / Be angry when you will, it shall have scope; / Do what you will, dishonour shall be humour. / O Cassius, you are yoked with a lamb / That carries anger as the flint bears fire, / Who, much enforced, shows a hasty spark, / And straight is cold again.

Put your dagger away. Be angry when you like, it will be allowed. Do what you like, your insults will be put down to your mood. Oh, Cassius, you are yoked together with a lamb who carries anger as flint carries fire: struck hard, it gives off a quick spark and is cold again at once.
Hath Cassius liv'd / To be but mirth and laughter to his Brutus, / When grief and blood ill-temper'd vexeth him?
Has Cassius lived only to be a joke and a laughing stock to his Brutus, when grief and bad temper trouble him?
When I spoke that, I was ill-temper'd too.
When I said that, I was bad-tempered too.
Do you confess so much? Give me your hand.
Do you admit that much? Give me your hand.
Have not you love enough to bear with me, / When that rash humour which my mother gave me / Makes me forgetful?
Don't you love me enough to be patient with me when the hot temper my mother gave me makes me forget myself?
Yes, Cassius; and from henceforth, / When you are over-earnest with your Brutus, / He'll think your mother chides, and leave you so.
Yes, Cassius. And from now on, when you are too harsh with your Brutus, he'll think it's your mother scolding and leave it at that.
[Within] Let me go in to see the generals, / There is some grudge between 'em; 'tis not meet / They be alone.
[Within] Let me in to see the generals. There is some quarrel between them. It isn't right for them to be alone.
[Within] You shall not come to them.
[Within] You shall not go to them.
[Within] Nothing but death shall stay me.
[Within] Nothing but death will stop me.
For shame, you generals! What do you mean? / Love, and be friends, as two such men should be; / For I have seen more years, I'm sure, than ye.
Shame on you, generals! What do you think you're doing? Love each other and be friends, as two such men should be, because I've seen more years than you, I'm sure.
Ha, ha! How vilely doth this cynic rhyme!
Ha, ha! How badly this rude philosopher rhymes!
Get you hence, sirrah. Saucy fellow, hence!
Get out of here, fellow. Cheeky man, get out!
Bear with him, Brutus; 'tis his fashion.
Put up with him, Brutus. It's his way.
I'll know his humour when he knows his time. / What should the wars do with these jigging fools? / Companion, hence!
I'll put up with his whims when he knows the right time for them. What use are these jingling fools in a war? Get out, fellow!
Lucilius and Titinius, bid the commanders / Prepare to lodge their companies tonight.
Lucilius and Titinius, tell the commanders to get their troops ready to camp for the night.
And come yourselves and bring Messala with you / Immediately to us.
And come back yourselves, and bring Messala with you to us at once.
I did not think you could have been so angry.
I didn't think you could be so angry.
O Cassius, I am sick of many griefs.
Oh, Cassius, I am sick with many sorrows.
Of your philosophy you make no use, / If you give place to accidental evils.
You're not making any use of your philosophy if you give in to the evils that chance brings.
No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.
No man bears sorrow better. Portia is dead.
How 'scap'd I killing, when I cross'd you so? / O insupportable and touching loss! / Upon what sickness?
How did I escape being killed when I crossed you like that? Oh, unbearable and painful loss! What illness was it?

Impatient of my absence, / And grief that young Octavius with Mark Antony / Have made themselves so strong; for with her death / That tidings came. With this she fell distract, / And, her attendants absent, swallow'd fire.

She couldn't bear my absence, and she grieved that young Octavius and Mark Antony had made themselves so strong, because that news came with the news of her death. At this she went out of her mind and, while her servants were away, swallowed burning coals.
Speak no more of her. Give me a bowl of wine. / In this I bury all unkindness, Cassius.
Don't talk about her any more. Give me a bowl of wine. In this I bury all our unkindness, Cassius.
