My heart is thirsty for that noble pledge. / Fill, Lucius, till the wine o'erswell the cup. / I cannot drink too much of Brutus' love.
My heart is thirsty for that noble toast. Fill it, Lucius, until the wine overflows the cup. I can't drink too much of Brutus's love.
Come in, Titinius! / Welcome, good Messala. / Now sit we close about this taper here, / And call in question our necessities.
Come in, Titinius! Welcome, good Messala. Now let's sit close round this candle here and discuss what we need to do.
No more, I pray you. / Messala, I have here received letters, / That young Octavius and Mark Antony / Come down upon us with a mighty power, / Bending their expedition toward Philippi.
No more, please. Messala, I have received letters here saying that young Octavius and Mark Antony are coming down on us with a mighty army, heading their expedition towards Philippi.
Myself have letters of the selfsame tenor.
I have letters saying the very same.
That by proscription and bills of outlawry / Octavius, Antony, and Lepidus / Have put to death an hundred Senators.
That by death lists and decrees of outlawry Octavius, Antony and Lepidus have put a hundred senators to death.
Therein our letters do not well agree. / Mine speak of seventy Senators that died / By their proscriptions, Cicero being one.
Our letters don't agree there. Mine speak of seventy senators who died on their death lists, Cicero among them.
Cicero is dead, / And by that order of proscription. / Had you your letters from your wife, my lord?
Cicero is dead, and by that same death list. Did you have letters from your wife, my lord?
Nor nothing in your letters writ of her?
And nothing written about her in your letters?
Why ask you? Hear you aught of her in yours?
Why do you ask? Do you hear anything about her in yours?
Now as you are a Roman, tell me true.
Now, as you are a Roman, tell me the truth.
Then like a Roman bear the truth I tell, / For certain she is dead, and by strange manner.
Then bear the truth I tell you like a Roman: she is certainly dead, and in a strange way.
Why, farewell, Portia. We must die, Messala. / With meditating that she must die once, / I have the patience to endure it now.
Why, farewell, Portia. We must all die, Messala. By thinking that she had to die some time, I have the patience to bear it now.
Even so great men great losses should endure.
That is how great men should bear great losses.
I have as much of this in art as you, / But yet my nature could not bear it so.
I know as much of this philosophy as you do, but my nature couldn't bear it like that.
Well, to our work alive. What do you think / Of marching to Philippi presently?
Well, to our work among the living. What do you think of marching to Philippi at once?
I do not think it good.
I don't think it's a good idea.
This it is: / 'Tis better that the enemy seek us; / So shall he waste his means, weary his soldiers, / Doing himself offence, whilst we, lying still, / Are full of rest, defence, and nimbleness.

It's this. It's better that the enemy should come looking for us. That way he will use up his supplies and tire his soldiers, harming himself, while we stay put, well rested, ready to defend ourselves and quick to move.

Good reasons must of force give place to better. / The people 'twixt Philippi and this ground / Do stand but in a forced affection; / For they have grudg'd us contribution. / The enemy, marching along by them, / By them shall make a fuller number up, / Come on refresh'd, new-added, and encourag'd; / From which advantage shall we cut him off / If at Philippi we do face him there, / These people at our back.

Good reasons must give way to better ones. The people between Philippi and here are only on our side because they have been forced to be, since they have resented giving us supplies. The enemy, marching through their country, will add to his numbers from them and come on refreshed, reinforced and encouraged. We will cut him off from that advantage if we face him at Philippi, with these people behind us.

Under your pardon. You must note besides, / That we have tried the utmost of our friends, / Our legions are brim-full, our cause is ripe. / The enemy increaseth every day; / We, at the height, are ready to decline. / There is a tide in the affairs of men, / Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune; / Omitted, all the voyage of their life / Is bound in shallows and in miseries. / On such a full sea are we now afloat, / And we must take the current when it serves, / Or lose our ventures.

Excuse me. You must also bear in mind that we have got all we can from our friends. Our legions are full to the brim, our cause is ripe. The enemy grows stronger every day; we, at our peak, are about to decline. There is a tide in the affairs of men which, taken at high water, leads on to fortune. If it is missed, the whole voyage of their life is stuck in shallows and misery. We are now afloat on such a high sea, and we must take the current while it is with us or lose everything we have risked.
Then, with your will, go on: / We'll along ourselves, and meet them at Philippi.
Then, as you wish, go on. We'll go ourselves and meet them at Philippi.
The deep of night is crept upon our talk, / And nature must obey necessity, / Which we will niggard with a little rest. / There is no more to say?
It has grown late at night while we've been talking, and our bodies must give in to their needs, which we will grudgingly satisfy with a little rest. Is there anything more to say?
No more. Good night: / Early tomorrow will we rise, and hence.
No more. Good night. We'll get up early tomorrow and go.
Farewell now, good Messala. / Good night, Titinius. Noble, noble Cassius, / Good night, and good repose.
Goodbye now, good Messala. Good night, Titinius. Noble, noble Cassius, good night, and rest well.
O my dear brother! / This was an ill beginning of the night. / Never come such division 'tween our souls! / Let it not, Brutus.
Oh, my dear brother! This was a bad start to the night. Let such a division never come between our souls again! Don't let it, Brutus.
Give me the gown. Where is thy instrument?
Give me the gown. Where is your instrument?
What, thou speak'st drowsily? / Poor knave, I blame thee not, thou art o'er-watch'd. / Call Claudius and some other of my men; / I'll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.
What, you sound sleepy? Poor boy, I don't blame you. You've stayed awake too long. Call Claudius and some of my other men. I'll have them sleep on cushions in my tent.
I pray you, sirs, lie in my tent and sleep; / It may be I shall raise you by-and-by / On business to my brother Cassius.
Please, sirs, lie down in my tent and sleep. I may wake you soon to send you on business to my brother Cassius.
So please you, we will stand and watch your pleasure.
If you like, we'll stand and stay awake ready for your orders.
I will not have it so; lie down, good sirs, / It may be I shall otherwise bethink me. / Look, Lucius, here's the book I sought for so; / I put it in the pocket of my gown.
I won't have that. Lie down, good sirs. I may change my mind. Look, Lucius, here's the book I was searching for. I put it in the pocket of my gown.
I was sure your lordship did not give it me.
I was sure your lordship didn't give it to me.
Bear with me, good boy, I am much forgetful. / Canst thou hold up thy heavy eyes awhile, / And touch thy instrument a strain or two?
Be patient with me, good boy, I'm very forgetful. Can you keep your heavy eyes open a little longer and play a tune or two on your instrument?
Ay, my lord, an't please you.
Yes, my lord, if you'd like.
It does, my boy. / I trouble thee too much, but thou art willing.
I would, my boy. I trouble you too much, but you are willing.
I should not urge thy duty past thy might; / I know young bloods look for a time of rest.
I shouldn't push your duty beyond your strength. I know young people need their time to rest.
I have slept, my lord, already.
I have slept already, my lord.
It was well done, and thou shalt sleep again; / I will not hold thee long. If I do live, / I will be good to thee.
That was well done, and you shall sleep again. I won't keep you long. If I live, I'll be good to you.

This is a sleepy tune. O murd'rous slumber, / Layest thou thy leaden mace upon my boy, / That plays thee music? Gentle knave, good night; / I will not do thee so much wrong to wake thee. / If thou dost nod, thou break'st thy instrument; / I'll take it from thee; and, good boy, good night. / Let me see, let me see; is not the leaf turn'd down / Where I left reading? Here it is, I think.

This is a sleepy tune. Oh, murderous sleep, are you laying your heavy club on my boy, who plays music for you? Gentle boy, good night. I won't do you the wrong of waking you. If you nod, you'll break your instrument. I'll take it from you, and, good boy, good night. Let me see, let me see. Isn't the page turned down where I stopped reading? Here it is, I think.

How ill this taper burns! Ha! who comes here? / I think it is the weakness of mine eyes / That shapes this monstrous apparition. / It comes upon me. Art thou anything? / Art thou some god, some angel, or some devil, / That mak'st my blood cold and my hair to stare? / Speak to me what thou art.

How badly this candle burns! Ha! Who's coming here? I think it's the weakness of my eyes that creates this monstrous ghost. It's coming towards me. Are you anything real? Are you some god, some angel or some devil, that makes my blood run cold and my hair stand on end? Tell me what you are.
To tell thee thou shalt see me at Philippi.
To tell you that you will see me at Philippi.
Well; then I shall see thee again?
Well, then I'll see you again?
Why, I will see thee at Philippi then.
Why, then I'll see you at Philippi.
Now I have taken heart, thou vanishest. / Ill spirit, I would hold more talk with thee. / Boy! Lucius! Varro! Claudius! Sirs, awake! Claudius!
Now that I have got my courage back, you vanish. Evil spirit, I would like to talk with you more. Boy! Lucius! Varro! Claudius! Sirs, wake up! Claudius!
The strings, my lord, are false.
The strings are out of tune, my lord.
He thinks he still is at his instrument. / Lucius, awake!
He thinks he's still playing his instrument. Lucius, wake up!
Didst thou dream, Lucius, that thou so criedst out?
Were you dreaming, Lucius, that you cried out like that?
My lord, I do not know that I did cry.
My lord, I don't know that I did cry out.
Yes, that thou didst. Didst thou see anything?
Yes, you did. Did you see anything?
Sleep again, Lucius. Sirrah Claudius! / Fellow thou, awake!
Go back to sleep, Lucius. Claudius, you there! You, fellow, wake up!
Why did you so cry out, sirs, in your sleep?
Why did you cry out like that in your sleep, sirs?
No, my lord, I saw nothing.
No, my lord, I saw nothing.
Go and commend me to my brother Cassius; / Bid him set on his powers betimes before, / And we will follow.
Go and give my greetings to my brother Cassius. Tell him to set his forces moving early, ahead of us, and we'll follow.
It shall be done, my lord.
It will be done, my lord.

Now, Antony, our hopes are answered. / You said the enemy would not come down, / But keep the hills and upper regions. / It proves not so; their battles are at hand, / They mean to warn us at Philippi here, / Answering before we do demand of them.

Now, Antony, our hopes have come true. You said the enemy wouldn't come down but would stay on the hills and the high ground. It's turned out otherwise. Their armies are close by. They mean to challenge us here at Philippi, responding before we have even challenged them.

Tut, I am in their bosoms, and I know / Wherefore they do it. They could be content / To visit other places, and come down / With fearful bravery, thinking by this face / To fasten in our thoughts that they have courage; / But 'tis not so.

Bah, I know what they're thinking, and I know why they're doing it. They would be happy to be somewhere else, and they come down with a show of courage that hides their fear, thinking that by putting on this face they will convince us they are brave. But it isn't so.
Prepare you, generals. / The enemy comes on in gallant show; / Their bloody sign of battle is hung out, / And something to be done immediately.
Get ready, generals. The enemy is coming on in a fine show. Their red flag of battle is hung out, and something must be done at once.
Octavius, lead your battle softly on / Upon the left hand of the even field.
Octavius, lead your army slowly forward on the left side of the level field.
Upon the right hand I. Keep thou the left.
I'll take the right. You keep the left.
Why do you cross me in this exigent?
Why do you contradict me at this critical moment?
I do not cross you; but I will do so.
I'm not contradicting you, but I will do it my way.
They stand, and would have parley.
They have stopped and want to talk.
Stand fast, Titinius; we must out and talk.
Stand firm, Titinius. We must go out and talk.
Mark Antony, shall we give sign of battle?
Mark Antony, shall we give the signal for battle?
No, Caesar, we will answer on their charge. / Make forth; the generals would have some words.
No, Caesar, we'll respond when they charge. Go forward. The generals want a few words.
Words before blows: is it so, countrymen?
Words before blows. Is that it, countrymen?
Not that we love words better, as you do.
Not that we love words more, as you do.
Good words are better than bad strokes, Octavius.
Good words are better than bad blows, Octavius.
In your bad strokes, Brutus, you give good words; / Witness the hole you made in Caesar's heart, / Crying, "Long live! Hail, Caesar!"
With your bad blows, Brutus, you give good words. Look at the hole you made in Caesar's heart while crying, "Long live Caesar! Hail, Caesar!"
Antony, / The posture of your blows are yet unknown; / But for your words, they rob the Hybla bees, / And leave them honeyless.
Antony, we don't yet know what kind of blows you strike. But as for your words, they rob the bees of Hybla and leave them without honey.
O yes, and soundless too, / For you have stol'n their buzzing, Antony, / And very wisely threat before you sting.
Oh yes, and without sound too, because you have stolen their buzzing, Antony, and very wisely you threaten before you sting.

Villains, you did not so when your vile daggers / Hack'd one another in the sides of Caesar: / You show'd your teeth like apes, and fawn'd like hounds, / And bow'd like bondmen, kissing Caesar's feet; / Whilst damned Casca, like a cur, behind / Struck Caesar on the neck. O you flatterers!

Villains, you didn't do that when your vile daggers hacked into one another in Caesar's sides. You grinned like apes, fawned like dogs and bowed like slaves, kissing Caesar's feet, while damned Casca, like a mongrel, struck Caesar on the neck from behind. Oh, you flatterers!
Flatterers! Now, Brutus, thank yourself. / This tongue had not offended so today, / If Cassius might have rul'd.
Flatterers! Now, Brutus, you can thank yourself. This tongue wouldn't be insulting us like this today if Cassius had had his way.

Come, come, the cause. If arguing makes us sweat, / The proof of it will turn to redder drops. / Look, I draw a sword against conspirators. / When think you that the sword goes up again? / Never, till Caesar's three and thirty wounds / Be well aveng'd; or till another Caesar / Have added slaughter to the sword of traitors.

Come, come, to the point. If arguing makes us sweat, the test of it will turn into redder drops. Look, I draw my sword against conspirators. When do you think this sword will go back in its sheath? Never, until Caesar's thirty-three wounds are fully avenged, or until another Caesar has been slaughtered by the swords of traitors too.
Caesar, thou canst not die by traitors' hands, / Unless thou bring'st them with thee.
Caesar, you can't die by traitors' hands unless you have brought them with you.
So I hope. / I was not born to die on Brutus' sword.
I hope so. I wasn't born to die on Brutus's sword.
O, if thou wert the noblest of thy strain, / Young man, thou couldst not die more honourable.
Oh, if you were the noblest of your family, young man, you couldn't die more honourably.
A peevish school-boy, worthless of such honour, / Join'd with a masker and a reveller.
A sulky schoolboy, not worthy of such an honour, teamed up with a party-goer and a drunkard.
Come, Antony; away! / Defiance, traitors, hurl we in your teeth. / If you dare fight today, come to the field; / If not, when you have stomachs.
Come, Antony, away! Traitors, we throw our defiance in your teeth. If you dare to fight today, come to the battlefield. If not, come when you have the stomach for it.
Why now, blow wind, swell billow, and swim bark! / The storm is up, and all is on the hazard.
Well now, blow, wind! Swell, wave! Sail, ship! The storm has started, and everything is at stake.
Ho, Lucilius! Hark, a word with you.
Hey, Lucilius! Listen, a word with you.

Messala, / This is my birth-day; as this very day / Was Cassius born. Give me thy hand, Messala: / Be thou my witness that against my will / As Pompey was, am I compell'd to set / Upon one battle all our liberties. / You know that I held Epicurus strong, / And his opinion. Now I change my mind, / And partly credit things that do presage. / Coming from Sardis, on our former ensign / Two mighty eagles fell, and there they perch'd, / Gorging and feeding from our soldiers' hands, / Who to Philippi here consorted us. / This morning are they fled away and gone, / And in their steads do ravens, crows, and kites / Fly o'er our heads, and downward look on us, / As we were sickly prey: their shadows seem / A canopy most fatal, under which / Our army lies, ready to give up the ghost.

Messala, this is my birthday. Cassius was born on this very day. Give me your hand, Messala. Be my witness that, against my will, as Pompey was, I am forced to risk all our freedom on one battle. You know I strongly believed in Epicurus and his teaching that omens mean nothing. Now I have changed my mind, and partly believe in signs that predict the future. On the way from Sardis, two mighty eagles swooped down on our front flag and perched there, gorging and feeding from our soldiers' hands, and they came with us here to Philippi. This morning they have flown away and gone, and in their place ravens, crows and kites fly over our heads and look down on us as if we were sickly prey. Their shadows seem a deadly canopy, under which our army lies, ready to die.
I but believe it partly, / For I am fresh of spirit, and resolv'd / To meet all perils very constantly.
I only partly believe it, because my spirit is fresh and I am determined to meet every danger very firmly.

Now, most noble Brutus, / The gods today stand friendly, that we may, / Lovers in peace, lead on our days to age! / But, since the affairs of men rest still incertain, / Let's reason with the worst that may befall. / If we do lose this battle, then is this / The very last time we shall speak together: / What are you then determined to do?

Now, most noble Brutus, may the gods be friendly today, so that we may live on, friends in peace, to old age! But since men's affairs are always uncertain, let's think about the worst that could happen. If we lose this battle, then this is the very last time we'll speak together. What are you determined to do then?

Even by the rule of that philosophy / By which I did blame Cato for the death / Which he did give himself, I know not how, / But I do find it cowardly and vile, / For fear of what might fall, so to prevent / The time of life, arming myself with patience / To stay the providence of some high powers / That govern us below.

I'll follow the rules of the philosophy by which I blamed Cato for killing himself. I don't know why, but I find it cowardly and vile to cut life short for fear of what might happen. Instead I'll arm myself with patience to wait for whatever the high powers that rule us here below have in store.
Then, if we lose this battle, / You are contented to be led in triumph / Thorough the streets of Rome?
Then if we lose this battle, you are content to be led as a prisoner in a triumphal parade through the streets of Rome?

No, Cassius, no: think not, thou noble Roman, / That ever Brutus will go bound to Rome; / He bears too great a mind. But this same day / Must end that work the Ides of March begun; / And whether we shall meet again I know not. / Therefore our everlasting farewell take. / For ever, and for ever, farewell, Cassius. / If we do meet again, why, we shall smile; / If not, why then this parting was well made.

No, Cassius, no. Don't think, you noble Roman, that Brutus will ever go to Rome in chains. His mind is too great for that. But this same day must finish the work that the fifteenth of March began, and I don't know whether we shall meet again. So take my everlasting farewell. For ever, and for ever, farewell, Cassius. If we meet again, why, we'll smile. If not, then this parting was well done.
For ever and for ever farewell, Brutus. / If we do meet again, we'll smile indeed; / If not, 'tis true this parting was well made.
For ever and for ever, farewell, Brutus. If we meet again, we'll smile indeed. If not, it's true this parting was well done.
Why then, lead on. O, that a man might know / The end of this day's business ere it come! / But it sufficeth that the day will end, / And then the end is known. Come, ho! away!
Then lead on. Oh, if only a man could know how this day's business will end before it comes! But it's enough that the day will end, and then the end will be known. Come on, away!
Ride, ride, Messala, ride, and give these bills / Unto the legions on the other side.
Ride, ride, Messala, ride, and give these orders to the legions on the other side.
Let them set on at once; for I perceive / But cold demeanor in Octavius' wing, / And sudden push gives them the overthrow. / Ride, ride, Messala; let them all come down.
Let them attack at once, because I see only a lack of fighting spirit in Octavius's wing, and a sudden push will overthrow them. Ride, ride, Messala. Let them all come down.
O, look, Titinius, look, the villains fly! / Myself have to mine own turn'd enemy: / This ensign here of mine was turning back; / I slew the coward, and did take it from him.
Oh, look, Titinius, look, the villains are running away! I have turned enemy to my own men. This standard-bearer of mine was turning back. I killed the coward and took the flag from him.
O Cassius, Brutus gave the word too early, / Who, having some advantage on Octavius, / Took it too eagerly: his soldiers fell to spoil, / Whilst we by Antony are all enclos'd.
Oh, Cassius, Brutus gave the order too early. He had some advantage over Octavius and took it too eagerly. His soldiers started looting, while we are all surrounded by Antony.
Fly further off, my lord, fly further off; / Mark Antony is in your tents, my lord. / Fly, therefore, noble Cassius, fly far off.
Run further off, my lord, run further off. Mark Antony is in your tents, my lord. So run, noble Cassius, run far away.
This hill is far enough. Look, look, Titinius; / Are those my tents where I perceive the fire?
This hill is far enough. Look, look, Titinius. Are those my tents where I can see the fire?

Titinius, if thou lovest me, / Mount thou my horse and hide thy spurs in him, / Till he have brought thee up to yonder troops / And here again, that I may rest assur'd / Whether yond troops are friend or enemy.

Titinius, if you love me, get on my horse and dig your spurs into him until he has carried you to those troops over there and back again, so that I can know for certain whether those troops are friends or enemies.
I will be here again, even with a thought.
I'll be back here as fast as a thought.
Go, Pindarus, get higher on that hill, / My sight was ever thick. Regard Titinius, / And tell me what thou notest about the field.
Go, Pindarus, climb higher up that hill. My eyesight was always poor. Watch Titinius, and tell me what you see on the battlefield.
This day I breathed first. Time is come round, / And where I did begin, there shall I end. / My life is run his compass. Sirrah, what news?
On this day I was born. Time has come full circle, and where I began, there I will end. My life has run its course. You there, what news?
[Above] Titinius is enclosed round about / With horsemen, that make to him on the spur, / Yet he spurs on. Now they are almost on him. / Now, Titinius! Now some light. O, he lights too. / He's ta'en!

[Above] Titinius is surrounded by horsemen riding at full speed towards him, and still he spurs on. Now they're almost on him. Come on, Titinius! Now some of them get off their horses. Oh, he gets off too. He's taken!
And, hark! they shout for joy.
And listen! They're shouting for joy.
Come down; behold no more. / O, coward that I am, to live so long, / To see my best friend ta'en before my face!
Come down. Don't watch any more. Oh, what a coward I am to live long enough to see my best friend taken in front of my eyes!

Come hither, sirrah. / In Parthia did I take thee prisoner; / And then I swore thee, saving of thy life, / That whatsoever I did bid thee do, / Thou shouldst attempt it. Come now, keep thine oath. / Now be a freeman; and with this good sword, / That ran through Caesar's bowels, search this bosom. / Stand not to answer. Here, take thou the hilts; / And when my face is cover'd, as 'tis now, / Guide thou the sword.—Caesar, thou art reveng'd, / Even with the sword that kill'd thee.

Come here, you. In Parthia I took you prisoner, and then, in return for sparing your life, I made you swear that whatever I told you to do, you would attempt it. Come now, keep your oath. Now be a free man, and with this good sword, which ran through Caesar's guts, search out this heart. Don't stop to answer. Here, take the hilt, and when my face is covered, as it is now, guide the sword. Caesar, you are avenged, with the very sword that killed you.
So, I am free, yet would not so have been, / Durst I have done my will. O Cassius! / Far from this country Pindarus shall run, / Where never Roman shall take note of him.
So I'm free, and yet I wouldn't have been free like this if I had dared to do what I wanted. Oh, Cassius! Pindarus will run far from this country, where no Roman will ever notice him.
It is but change, Titinius; for Octavius / Is overthrown by noble Brutus' power, / As Cassius' legions are by Antony.
It's only an exchange, Titinius, because Octavius has been beaten by noble Brutus's forces, just as Cassius's legions have been by Antony.
These tidings would well comfort Cassius.
This news will be a great comfort to Cassius.
All disconsolate, / With Pindarus his bondman, on this hill.
Completely in despair, with Pindarus, his slave, on this hill.
Is not that he that lies upon the ground?
Isn't that him lying on the ground?
He lies not like the living. O my heart!
He isn't lying like a living man. Oh, my heart!

No, this was he, Messala, / But Cassius is no more. O setting sun, / As in thy red rays thou dost sink to night, / So in his red blood Cassius' day is set. / The sun of Rome is set. Our day is gone; / Clouds, dews, and dangers come; our deeds are done. / Mistrust of my success hath done this deed.

No, this was him, Messala, but Cassius is no more. Oh, setting sun, just as you sink into night in your red rays, so Cassius's day has set in his red blood. The sun of Rome has set. Our day is over. Clouds, dews and dangers are coming. Our deeds are done. Doubt about how my mission would turn out has done this.

Mistrust of good success hath done this deed. / O hateful Error, Melancholy's child! / Why dost thou show to the apt thoughts of men / The things that are not? O Error, soon conceiv'd, / Thou never com'st unto a happy birth, / But kill'st the mother that engender'd thee!

Doubt about our success has done this. Oh, hateful error, child of melancholy! Why do you show men's ready imaginations things that aren't true? Oh, error, so quickly conceived, you never come to a happy birth, but kill the mother who gave birth to you!
What, Pindarus! where art thou, Pindarus?

Seek him, Titinius, whilst I go to meet / The noble Brutus, thrusting this report / Into his ears. I may say thrusting it; / For piercing steel and darts envenomed / Shall be as welcome to the ears of Brutus / As tidings of this sight.

Look for him, Titinius, while I go to meet noble Brutus and thrust this news into his ears. I may well say thrust it, because piercing steel and poisoned darts would be as welcome to Brutus's ears as news of this sight.
Hie you, Messala, / And I will seek for Pindarus the while.
Hurry, Messala, and I'll look for Pindarus meanwhile.

Why didst thou send me forth, brave Cassius? / Did I not meet thy friends? And did not they / Put on my brows this wreath of victory, / And bid me give it thee? Didst thou not hear their shouts? / Alas, thou hast misconstrued everything! / But, hold thee, take this garland on thy brow; / Thy Brutus bid me give it thee, and I / Will do his bidding. Brutus, come apace, / And see how I regarded Caius Cassius. / By your leave, gods. This is a Roman's part. / Come, Cassius' sword, and find Titinius' heart.

Why did you send me out, brave Cassius? Didn't I meet your friends? And didn't they put this victory wreath on my head and tell me to give it to you? Didn't you hear their shouts? Oh, you misunderstood everything! But wait, take this garland on your head. Your Brutus told me to give it to you, and I will do what he told me. Brutus, come quickly and see how I honoured Caius Cassius. With your permission, gods: this is a Roman's role. Come, Cassius's sword, and find Titinius's heart.
Where, where, Messala, doth his body lie?
Where, where, Messala, is his body lying?
Lo, yonder, and Titinius mourning it.
Look, over there, and Titinius mourning over it.
O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet! / Thy spirit walks abroad, and turns our swords / In our own proper entrails.
Oh, Julius Caesar, you are still mighty! Your spirit walks abroad and turns our swords into our own guts.
Brave Titinius! / Look whether he have not crown'd dead Cassius!
Brave Titinius! Look how he has crowned dead Cassius!

Are yet two Romans living such as these? / The last of all the Romans, fare thee well! / It is impossible that ever Rome / Should breed thy fellow. Friends, I owe more tears / To this dead man than you shall see me pay. / I shall find time, Cassius, I shall find time. / Come therefore, and to Thassos send his body. / His funerals shall not be in our camp, / Lest it discomfort us. Lucilius, come; / And come, young Cato; let us to the field. / Labeo and Flavius, set our battles on. / 'Tis three o'clock; and Romans, yet ere night / We shall try fortune in a second fight.

Are there still two Romans alive like these? The last of all the Romans, farewell! It is impossible that Rome should ever produce your equal. Friends, I owe more tears to this dead man than you will see me pay. I'll find time, Cassius, I'll find time. So come, and send his body to Thassos. His funeral must not be held in our camp, in case it disheartens us. Lucilius, come, and come, young Cato. Let's go to the battlefield. Labeo and Flavius, move our armies forward. It's three o'clock, and, Romans, before night we will try our luck in a second fight.
Yet, countrymen, O, yet hold up your heads!
Still, countrymen, oh, still hold up your heads!

What bastard doth not? Who will go with me? / I will proclaim my name about the field. / I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho! / A foe to tyrants, and my country's friend. / I am the son of Marcus Cato, ho!

Who is so low-born that he wouldn't? Who will come with me? I'll announce my name all over the battlefield. I am the son of Marcus Cato! An enemy of tyrants, and my country's friend. I am the son of Marcus Cato!
And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I; / Brutus, my country's friend; know me for Brutus!
And I am Brutus, Marcus Brutus, I am. Brutus, my country's friend. Know me as Brutus!
O young and noble Cato, art thou down? / Why, now thou diest as bravely as Titinius, / And mayst be honour'd, being Cato's son.
Oh, young and noble Cato, are you down? Why, now you die as bravely as Titinius, and you may be honoured as Cato's son.
Only I yield to die: / There is so much that thou wilt kill me straight;
I surrender only to die. Here is plenty to persuade you to kill me at once.
Kill Brutus, and be honour'd in his death.
Kill Brutus, and be honoured for his death.
We must not. A noble prisoner!
Room, ho! Tell Antony, Brutus is ta'en.
Make way! Tell Antony that Brutus has been captured.
I'll tell the news. Here comes the General.
I'll tell him the news. Here comes the general.
Brutus is ta'en, Brutus is ta'en, my lord.
Brutus is captured, Brutus is captured, my lord.

Safe, Antony; Brutus is safe enough. / I dare assure thee that no enemy / Shall ever take alive the noble Brutus. / The gods defend him from so great a shame! / When you do find him, or alive or dead, / He will be found like Brutus, like himself.

Safe, Antony. Brutus is safe enough. I promise you that no enemy will ever take noble Brutus alive. May the gods protect him from such a great shame! When you find him, alive or dead, he will be found behaving like Brutus, like himself.

This is not Brutus, friend; but, I assure you, / A prize no less in worth. Keep this man safe, / Give him all kindness. I had rather have / Such men my friends than enemies. Go on, / And see whether Brutus be alive or dead; / And bring us word unto Octavius' tent / How everything is chanc'd.

This isn't Brutus, friend, but, I assure you, a prize just as valuable. Keep this man safe. Treat him with every kindness. I'd rather have such men as friends than enemies. Go on and see whether Brutus is alive or dead, and bring us word in Octavius's tent of how everything has turned out.
Come, poor remains of friends, rest on this rock.
Come, poor remnants of my friends, rest on this rock.
Statilius show'd the torch-light; but, my lord, / He came not back: he is or ta'en or slain.
Statilius showed his torch as a signal, but, my lord, he didn't come back. He's either captured or killed.
Sit thee down, Clitus. Slaying is the word; / It is a deed in fashion. Hark thee, Clitus.
Sit down, Clitus. Killed is the word. It's the fashionable thing to do. Listen, Clitus.
What, I, my lord? No, not for all the world.
What, me, my lord? No, not for all the world.
Shall I do such a deed?
Shall I do such a deed?
What ill request did Brutus make to thee?
What evil request did Brutus make of you?
To kill him, Clitus. Look, he meditates.
To kill him, Clitus. Look, he's lost in thought.
Now is that noble vessel full of grief, / That it runs over even at his eyes.
Now that noble vessel is so full of grief that it overflows even at his eyes.
Come hither, good Volumnius; list a word.
Come here, good Volumnius. Listen to a word.
Why, this, Volumnius: / The ghost of Caesar hath appear'd to me / Two several times by night; at Sardis once, / And this last night here in Philippi fields. / I know my hour is come.
Why, this, Volumnius. The ghost of Caesar has appeared to me twice at night: once at Sardis, and last night here on the fields of Philippi. I know my time has come.
Nay I am sure it is, Volumnius. / Thou seest the world, Volumnius, how it goes; / Our enemies have beat us to the pit.
No, I'm sure it has, Volumnius. You see how the world is going, Volumnius. Our enemies have driven us to the edge of the pit.

It is more worthy to leap in ourselves / Than tarry till they push us. Good Volumnius, / Thou know'st that we two went to school together; / Even for that our love of old, I pr'ythee / Hold thou my sword-hilts, whilst I run on it.

It is more honourable to leap in ourselves than to wait until they push us. Good Volumnius, you know we went to school together. For the sake of that old friendship, I beg you, hold my sword hilt while I run on it.
That's not an office for a friend, my lord.
That's no job for a friend, my lord.
Fly, fly, my lord! there is no tarrying here.
Run, run, my lord! You can't stay here.

Farewell to you; and you; and you, Volumnius. / Strato, thou hast been all this while asleep; / Farewell to thee too, Strato.—Countrymen, / My heart doth joy, that yet in all my life / I found no man but he was true to me. / I shall have glory by this losing day / More than Octavius and Mark Antony / By this vile conquest shall attain unto. / So fare you well at once; for Brutus' tongue / Hath almost ended his life's history. / Night hangs upon mine eyes; my bones would rest, / That have but labour'd to attain this hour.

Goodbye to you, and you, and you, Volumnius. Strato, you've been asleep all this time. Goodbye to you too, Strato. Countrymen, my heart is glad that in all my life I never found a man who wasn't true to me. I will have more glory from this day of defeat than Octavius and Mark Antony will gain by their vile victory. So goodbye to you all at once, because Brutus's tongue has almost finished telling the story of his life. Night hangs on my eyes. My bones want to rest, after working only to reach this hour.

I pr'ythee, Strato, stay thou by thy lord. / Thou art a fellow of a good respect; / Thy life hath had some smatch of honour in it. / Hold then my sword, and turn away thy face, / While I do run upon it. Wilt thou, Strato?
Please, Strato, stay with your lord. You are a man with a good reputation. Your life has had some taste of honour in it. So hold my sword and turn your face away while I run on it. Will you, Strato?
Give me your hand first. Fare you well, my lord.
Give me your hand first. Goodbye, my lord.
Farewell, good Strato.—Caesar, now be still: / I kill'd not thee with half so good a will.
Goodbye, good Strato. Caesar, now rest in peace. I didn't kill you half as willingly as I kill myself.
My master's man. Strato, where is thy master?
My master's servant. Strato, where is your master?
Free from the bondage you are in, Messala. / The conquerors can but make a fire of him; / For Brutus only overcame himself, / And no man else hath honour by his death.
Free from the slavery you are in, Messala. The winners can only burn his body, because only Brutus defeated Brutus, and no one else gets honour from his death.
So Brutus should be found. I thank thee, Brutus, / That thou hast prov'd Lucilius' saying true.
That is how Brutus should be found. Thank you, Brutus, for proving what Lucilius said was true.
All that serv'd Brutus, I will entertain them. / Fellow, wilt thou bestow thy time with me?
I'll take into my service all the men who served Brutus. Fellow, will you spend your time with me?
Ay, if Messala will prefer me to you.
Yes, if Messala will recommend me to you.
How did my master die, Strato?
I held the sword, and he did run on it.
I held the sword, and he ran on it.
Octavius, then take him to follow thee, / That did the latest service to my master.
Octavius, then take him into your service, the man who did the last service for my master.

This was the noblest Roman of them all. / All the conspirators save only he, / Did that they did in envy of great Caesar; / He only, in a general honest thought / And common good to all, made one of them. / His life was gentle, and the elements / So mix'd in him that Nature might stand up / And say to all the world, "This was a man!"

This was the noblest Roman of them all. All the conspirators except him did what they did out of envy of great Caesar. He alone joined them with honest thoughts for the general good of all. His life was gentle, and the elements were so well mixed in him that Nature could stand up and say to all the world, "This was a man!"

According to his virtue let us use him / With all respect and rites of burial. / Within my tent his bones tonight shall lie, / Most like a soldier, order'd honourably. / So call the field to rest, and let's away, / To part the glories of this happy day.

Let's treat him as his virtue deserves, with all respect and funeral rites. His body will lie in my tent tonight, laid out with honour like a soldier. So call off the army to rest, and let's go and share out the glories of this happy day.
